MOU = intent, typically not legally binding. BPA = partner responsibilities and profit sharing.
Supply chain analysis looks at the vendor's own vendors and components (e.g. SBOM).

briefing.title: Risk-score five vendors before contracts are signed
briefing.situation: Procurement has five vendors waiting for approval, including a payroll provider, an air-conditioning contractor and a managed IT provider that wants administrator access. Each vendor filled in a security questionnaire, and legal shared the contract clauses actually signed. We need a decision on each vendor before anyone gets access to our data or network.
your_task: Score each vendor's inherent risk from what it will touch: data sensitivity, type of access, and how critical the service is.
Reduce that score by how well the vendor's questionnaire answers show working controls, giving residual risk.
Check the contract for required clauses, such as right-to-audit, breach-notice time and uptime promises.
Decide APPROVE, APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS or REJECT, and set how often each vendor is reviewed.
briefing.why_it_matters: Many large breaches start at a supplier, not at the company itself. A vendor with administrator access and an undisclosed conflict of interest is a direct path into our network.
done_when: All 5 vendors have inherent and residual risk scores and a decision.
Every missing clause or questionnaire gap is listed as a condition.
The Identity and Access Management (IAM) team confirms no vendor account or privileged access is created for a rejected vendor (VN-3, VN-5).

glossary.Inherent risk: The risk before any controls are counted.
glossary.Residual risk: The risk left after the vendor's controls are taken into account.
glossary.SOC 2 / ISO 27001: Independent audits that show a company's security controls really work.
glossary.Right-to-audit clause: Contract wording that lets us inspect the vendor's security ourselves.
glossary.SLA (service level agreement): A contract promise about uptime and response times.
glossary.MOU vs BPA: An MOU (memorandum of understanding) states intent and is usually not binding; a BPA (business partners agreement) sets binding partner duties.

briefing.talking_point: Assessed 5 vendors on inherent and residual risk: approved 1, approved 2 with conditions, and rejected 2, including a managed IT provider seeking privileged access that had not disclosed a conflict of interest.

labs.title: Lab 16 — Security Control Classifier (category × type)
labs.objectives: SY0-701 1.1 Security control categories and types
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 1.1 Compare and contrast various types of security controls: categories (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and control types (preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating, directive).

How it classifies

Each description is scored against keyword/phrase weights in config/default_policies.json → control_classification (whole-word, case insensitive). Category and type are scored independently. The highest score wins only if it is UNIQUE; a tie or zero evidence returns Unclassified (deny by default: no guessing). Every result lists the phrases that drove it, so you can argue with the classifier, and improve the weights when it is wrong.

Run it

python main.py lab 16

insight.objective: SY0-701 1.1 Control categories (technical, managerial, operational, physical) and types.
concepts: CATEGORY = who/what implements it: technology (technical), people management and policy (managerial), people doing it (operational), the physical world (physical).
TYPE = what it does: prevent, deter, detect, correct, compensate for another control, or direct behaviour.
Every control has BOTH: a door lock is physical + preventive; a log review by managers is managerial + detective.
Compensating controls stand in when the primary control cannot be used (unpatchable server → isolate it).
failure_modes: Only buying preventive controls; nothing detects or corrects when prevention fails.
Writing policies (directive) with no technical enforcement or monitoring behind them.
Calling a compensating control 'temporary' and never removing the underlying gap.
Mapping controls inconsistently, so audits find gaps that were only labelling errors.
ai_governance: An AI GRC assistant can draft control mappings, but must show the evidence (phrases) behind each label.
Ambiguous controls should come back 'Unclassified' for a human, not be forced into a category.
AI agents themselves need controls of every type: preventive (allow-lists), detective (ledger), corrective (kill switch).
Policy statements for agents are directive; enforce them technically (Lab 5) or they are only wishes.
exam_tips: Signs: 'Authorized personnel only' = directive; 'trespassers will be prosecuted' = deterrent.
Backups/restore = corrective; logs/alarms/motion detectors = detective; firewall/locks = preventive.
Guards on patrol = operational (people performing the control).
Separation of duties is managerial; used in place of a missing control it becomes compensating.

briefing.title: Tag the 19 controls in our control library by category and type
briefing.situation: Our control library lists 19 security measures in plain sentences, from firewall rules to door locks to a weekly manager review of login reports. Auditors want each one tagged two ways: what kind of control it is, and what job it does. One entry is just a note about our cloud platform and may not be a control at all.
your_task: Read each control description and match key phrases to a category: technical, physical, managerial or operational.
Match key phrases to a type: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating or directive.
Leave any entry with no matching phrases as Unclassified for a person to review.
Compare your tags with the answer key and record the score.
briefing.why_it_matters: Auditors check that every risk has controls that prevent, detect and correct problems. A library with wrong labels hides gaps, such as having lots of detection but nothing that fixes the damage afterward.
done_when: All 19 controls are tagged with a category and type, with the phrases that support each tag.
Entries with no supporting evidence are marked Unclassified instead of guessed.
Tags match the answer key, and identity controls (such as login logging and the weekly login report review) are listed for the IAM team's access review evidence.

glossary.Control category: Who or what carries out the control: technology, a physical object, management policy, or people following a procedure.
glossary.Preventive control: Stops a problem before it happens, like a door lock.
glossary.Detective control: Spots a problem while or after it happens, like a log or motion sensor.
glossary.Corrective control: Fixes the damage after a problem, like restoring from backup.
glossary.Compensating control: A substitute used when the normal control is not possible.
glossary.Directive control: Tells people what they must or must not do, like a policy or sign.

briefing.talking_point: Classified 19 security controls by category and type with 19/19 agreement with the answer key, and left the one entry with no supporting evidence as Unclassified for human review instead of guessing.

labs.title: Lab 17 — PKI & Certificate Validator
labs.objectives: SY0-701 1.4 PKI: CAs, chains, CRL/OCSP, wildcard/SAN, self-signed, key length, pinning
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 1.4 Use appropriate cryptographic solutions: public key infrastructure (public/private keys, key escrow), certificates (certificate authorities, CRLs, OCSP, self-signed, third-party, root of trust, CSR generation, wildcard), key length, algorithms.

What it does

A browser-style validator for TLS certificate chains. Certificates are structured JSON records (subject, issuer, serial, validity, key, signature algorithm, CA flag, SAN, EKU, SPKI hash), so the trust rules are visible instead of buried in ASN.1. For each connection it checks, deny by default:

1. Path & trust: each cert's issuer is the next cert's subject; every issuer is a CA; the chain ends at (or is issued by) a trusted root. → INCOMPLETE_CHAIN, NOT_A_CA, SELF_SIGNED, UNTRUSTED_ROOT 2. Validity: every cert is inside its notBefore/notAfter window. → EXPIRED, NOT_YET_VALID; warnings EXPIRING_SOON, VALIDITY_TOO_LONG (> 398 days) 3. Hostname: matches a SAN entry (CN only if there is no SAN). A wildcard covers exactly ONE label: *.example.com matches a.example.com but not a.b.example.com or example.com. → HOSTNAME_MISMATCH 4. Strength: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits; SHA-2 signatures only. → WEAK_KEY, WEAK_SIGNATURE 5. Usage: the leaf's EKU must include serverAuth. → WRONG_KEY_USAGE 6. Revocation: OCSP status or the issuer's CRL. → REVOKED; no status available → REVOCATION_UNKNOWN (a warning under soft-fail, an error under hard-fail) 7. Pinning: if the app pins SPKI hashes, the presented key must match. → PIN_MISMATCH (classic sign of TLS interception)

Verdict: UNTRUSTED (any error) / TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS / TRUSTED.

Run it

python main.py lab 17

insight.objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and revocation.
concepts: Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) → intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2 signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
failure_modes: Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings, which makes MITM attacks invisible.
Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a revoked certificate look fine.
Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a calendar reminder, not automation.
ai_governance: Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be configured with 'verify=False'.
An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop the agent, not be retried around.
Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
exam_tips: 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of revoked serials' = CRL.
'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists several different names' = SAN.
'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything else chains to.

briefing.title: Browsers and apps are showing certificate warnings on our sites
briefing.situation: Users report security warnings on several of our websites, the VPN (virtual private network) and the mobile banking app. We collected the certificate each server presented on ten connections, plus the revocation lists we could reach, as of 2026-11-03. We need to know which connections are safe and what is wrong with each of the others.
your_task: Check each connection's certificate chain back to a trusted root certificate authority.
Check expiry dates, whether the name matches the site, key strength and signature type.
Check revocation status with the CRL or OCSP, and check the mobile app's pinned keys.
Give each connection a verdict and a specific fix.
briefing.why_it_matters: An expired or revoked certificate can take an API (application programming interface) or the VPN offline, and a pin mismatch can mean someone is intercepting traffic. Teaching users to click through warnings makes real attacks easy.
done_when: All 10 connections have a verdict: TRUSTED, TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS or UNTRUSTED.
Each problem has a named fix, such as renewing, re-issuing with the right names, or sending the full chain.
The revoked VPN certificate (P-06) is escalated as a possible key compromise, and IAM is told so certificate-based sign-in to the VPN can be checked.

glossary.PKI (public key infrastructure): The system of certificates and authorities that proves a website or device is who it claims to be.
glossary.Certificate authority (CA): A trusted organization that issues and signs certificates.
glossary.Certificate chain: The links from a site's certificate up through intermediates to a trusted root.
glossary.Revocation (CRL / OCSP): Cancelling a certificate early; a CRL (certificate revocation list) or OCSP (online certificate status protocol) is how clients check.
glossary.Wildcard / SAN: Ways one certificate covers several names; a wildcard covers only one level of subdomain.
glossary.Certificate pinning: An app accepts only specific keys, so a swapped-in certificate is rejected.

briefing.talking_point: Validated 10 TLS (encrypted web) connections: 1 trusted, 1 trusted with warnings and 8 untrusted, finding an expired API certificate, a revoked VPN certificate, an overstretched wildcard, a missing intermediate, a self-signed console, weak RSA-1024 crypto, a leaf certificate misused as a CA and a pin mismatch that pointed to interception.

labs.title: Lab 18 — Data Protection & DLP Gate
labs.objectives: SY0-701 3.3 Data types, classifications, states, sovereignty, protection methods · 4.5 DLP · 5.4 Data sovereignty / privacy
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 3.3 Protect data: data types (regulated, trade secret, intellectual property, legal, financial, human/non-human readable), classifications (public, private, sensitive, confidential, restricted, critical), states of data (at rest, in transit, in use), data sovereignty, geolocation, methods (geographic restrictions, encryption, hashing, masking, tokenization, obfuscation, segmentation, permission restrictions).
  • 4.5 Data loss prevention (DLP) as an enterprise security capability.
  • 5.4 Privacy: data subject, data sovereignty and local/regional rules.

How it works

1. Detect: policy regexes scan each sample record for SSNs, payment card numbers (PAN, kept only if the Luhn check passes, so a random 16-digit order number is NOT flagged), health record IDs, emails, phones, passwords, API keys and trade-secret / IP / legal markings. Each detector maps to a data type and a classification. Records are the data BEFORE the flow's stated protection is applied. 2. Classify: effective classification = the highest of the declared label and every detected classification. An unknown declared label → BLOCK. 3. Gate each outbound flow, deny by default:

  • destination missing/unapproved, destination type not allowed for the classification, or region not allowed (geographic restriction) → BLOCK;
  • regulated personal data whose origin region has a sovereignty rule may only be processed in that rule's regions → BLOCK;
  • per data type × state, the applied protection must be an accepted method (an encrypted channel counts as encryption in transit). A miss is either a required fix (ALLOW_WITH_PROTECTION) or a hard BLOCK (e.g. passwords stored with reversible encryption instead of a salted hash).

Run it

python main.py lab 18

insight.objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states, sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
concepts: Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone typed; the label drives handling rules.
States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate, hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
failure_modes: Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you have every password (hash + salt instead).
A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking data sovereignty rules.
Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4 digits.
ai_governance: Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and PII must not reach an external model.
AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are data in transit and at rest too.
Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy' line in a record is data, not an instruction.
exam_tips: 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' = tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2), never encryption.
Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides; geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert, block or quarantine transfers.

briefing.title: Review eight outbound data flows before the new DLP gate goes live
briefing.situation: A retail company is turning on a data loss prevention (DLP) gate that checks data before it leaves a system. Eight flows are queued for review, including card payments, a payroll backup going overseas, a European customer list going to a US analytics tool, and a new service that stores passwords. Some flows are labelled with a lower sensitivity than the data inside them.
your_task: Scan each flow's content for card numbers, Social Security numbers, personal details, passwords, keys and trade secrets, and raise the label if needed.
Check each flow's data state, destination and region against policy, including data sovereignty rules.
Check that the protection fits the data: masking, tokenization, encryption, or hashing for passwords.
Decide ALLOW, ALLOW_WITH_PROTECTION or BLOCK for each flow.
briefing.why_it_matters: Sending card numbers or personal data to the wrong place can bring fines and breach notices. Passwords stored with reversible encryption can all be read at once if the key leaks.
done_when: All 8 flows have an effective label, a decision and a reason.
Flows whose content outranks their label are relabelled.
The password-storage flow (DF-6) is blocked until it uses salted hashing, and the IAM team signs off on the credential-storage design.

glossary.DLP (data loss prevention): Tools and rules that stop sensitive data from leaving where it should stay.
glossary.Data classification: A label for how sensitive data is, such as public, confidential or restricted.
glossary.Data sovereignty: Laws that say certain data must stay in a specific country or region.
glossary.Tokenization: Replacing a real value, like a card number, with a random stand-in.
glossary.Masking: Hiding most of a value on screen, like showing only the last four card digits.
glossary.Hashing: A one-way scramble; with a salt (random extra value) it is the right way to store passwords.

briefing.talking_point: Reviewed 8 outbound data flows: allowed 2, allowed 2 with added protection and blocked 4, including an EU customer list bound for a US tool, a payroll backup headed to an unapproved region and a service storing passwords with reversible encryption.

labs.title: Lab 19 — SIEM Correlation & Alert Tuning
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.4 Alerting and monitoring: SIEM, correlation, alert tuning, response · 4.9 Log data sources
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.4 Alerting and monitoring: monitoring computing resources (systems, applications, infrastructure); activities (log aggregation, alerting, scanning, reporting, archiving, alert response and remediation / validation, quarantine, alert tuning); tools (SIEM, SCAP, benchmarks, agents/agentless, SNMP traps, NetFlow, antivirus, DLP, vulnerability scanners).
  • 4.9 Data sources to support an investigation: firewall, application, endpoint, OS-specific security and network (DNS) logs.

Model

1. Normalise: every event needs id, ts (ISO-8601 UTC string or integer epoch seconds) and a known source. An event that fails is not dropped: it raises SIEM-000 (an unparsed event is invisible to every other rule). 2. Correlate: each rule in policies["siem"]["rules"] has a logic type — threshold (N events, or N distinct values, per group within W seconds; brute force escalates to critical if a success follows), impossible_travel, after_hours, source_silence (blind spot), threat_intel, match. 3. Tune: a suppression applies only if it matches the rule and entities, has an owner, and has not expired at the alert's time; critical alerts are never suppressed. Anything else leaves the alert standing (deny by default). 4. Score: each event carries a ground-truth scenario label, so the lab counts true / false positives, false negatives and precision before and after tuning.

Run it

python main.py lab 19

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.4 Alerting and monitoring: SIEM aggregation, correlation, alert tuning and response (with 4.9 log sources).
concepts: A SIEM aggregates and normalises logs from many sources so one rule can correlate auth, firewall, EDR, DNS and app events.
Correlation rules turn many weak signals into one alert: thresholds in a time window, distinct counts, travel speed, time of day.
Silence is a signal: an expected source that stops sending events is a monitoring blind spot, not a quiet day.
Alert tuning (thresholds, suppressions) cuts false positives; every suppression needs an owner, a reason and an expiry.
Alert response and remediation: quarantine via EDR, block at the firewall, lock the account, then validate the fix.
failure_modes: Alert fatigue: a noisy rule nobody tunes trains analysts to ignore the queue, real attacks included.
Permanent, ownerless suppressions: the scanner exception outlives the scanner and hides an attacker on that IP.
Dropping events the parser cannot read instead of alerting on them: a silent loss of visibility.
Over-tuning: raising a threshold to kill noise also hides low-and-slow attacks (false negatives).
ai_governance: An AI triage agent may close or suppress alerts only through owned, expiring, logged suppressions, never silently.
Score the agent like a rule: measure its precision and false negatives against labelled incidents before trusting it.
Containment actions (quarantine, account lock) recommended by an agent should need human approval or a tight playbook scope.
Event fields are untrusted input: a log line saying 'ignore previous instructions' must never steer the agent.
exam_tips: 'Collects logs from many systems and correlates them' = SIEM. 'Unsolicited alert from a network device' = SNMP trap.
'Who talked to whom, how much, which ports, but no payload' = NetFlow. 'Automates benchmark checks (XCCDF/OVAL)' = SCAP.
False positive = alert on benign activity; false negative = attack with no alert. Tuning trades one for the other.
Agent-based monitoring installs software on the host; agentless uses remote protocols or APIs.
Isolating an infected endpoint so it cannot spread = quarantine; rescanning afterwards = validation.

briefing.title: Overnight SIEM alerts: brute force, password spraying and impossible travel
briefing.situation: Our security monitoring system collected 52 log events overnight from sign-in, firewall, DNS (domain name system), endpoint and application sources. Several point to attacks on user accounts: repeated failed logins followed by a success, one address trying many accounts, and users signing in from two continents within an hour. We also suspect noisy alerts and a gap where one log source went quiet.
your_task: Correlate the 52 events into alerts using the detection rules.
Apply the suppression list, but only entries that have an owner and have not expired.
Write the response for each alert, such as disable the account, revoke sessions or quarantine the host.
Measure alert quality before and after tuning, and name any attack that no rule caught.
briefing.why_it_matters: A successful login right after a burst of failures may mean an attacker is already inside an account. Too many false alarms bury the real ones, and a silent log source is a blind spot.
done_when: All 12 alerts have a disposition, a reason and a response.
Only the owned, unexpired scanner suppression is applied; the expired and ownerless ones are ignored.

Account alerts (brute force on jdoe, spraying, impossible travel for bnguyen and asmith, after-hours admin grant by mlee) are handed to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) team for account disable, session revocation, multi-factor authentication (MFA) checks and access review.
The missed low-and-slow password guessing against pchan is logged as a detection gap.

glossary.SIEM: Security information and event management: a system that gathers logs and raises alerts.
glossary.Correlation rule: Logic that links related events, such as five failed logins in five minutes.
glossary.Brute force: Trying many passwords against one account.
glossary.Password spraying: Trying one or two common passwords against many accounts.
glossary.Impossible travel: Sign-ins from places too far apart to reach in the time between them.
glossary.Suppression: A rule that silences a known, harmless alert; it should have an owner and an end date.
glossary.Precision / recall: Precision is the share of alerts that were real; recall is the share of real attacks that raised an alert.

briefing.talking_point: Correlated 52 log events into 12 alerts, suppressed 1 authorized-scanner false positive to raise precision from 83.3% to 90.9%, sent the brute-force, spraying and impossible-travel account alerts to IAM for session revocation and MFA checks, and flagged a missed low-and-slow password attack as a detection gap.

labs.title: Lab 20 — Cloud Architecture & IaC Misconfiguration Gate
labs.objectives: SY0-701 3.1 Architecture models: cloud responsibility matrix, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA · 3.3 Data at rest/in transit · 4.1 Secure baselines · 4.6 Least privilege
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 3.1 Security implications of architecture models: cloud (responsibility matrix, hybrid, third-party vendors), infrastructure as code, serverless, microservices, network infrastructure (physical isolation/air-gapped, logical segmentation, SDN), on-premises, containerization, virtualization, IoT, ICS/SCADA, RTOS, embedded, high availability; considerations (availability, resilience, cost, ease of recovery, patch availability, inability to patch, ...).
  • 3.3 Protecting data: data at rest / in transit (encryption).
  • 4.1 Secure baselines and hardening of cloud infrastructure.
  • 4.6 Identity and access management: least privilege.

How it works

A pre-deployment policy-as-code gate over a simplified, Terraform-like plan (a list of resources {id, type, ...properties}). Every check in the policy names the resource types it covers, a property, an operator and a severity. A check passes only when the property is DECLARED and satisfies the operator; a missing property fails (deny by default). A resource type the policy has never reviewed is itself a finding.

resource  = PASS (no findings) / FAIL (one or more findings, each with a fix)
plan      = BLOCK if any critical, or more HIGH findings than allowed
            WARN  if any other finding
            PASS  otherwise

The policy also holds a shared-responsibility matrix (IaaS / PaaS / SaaS × layer) and a table of architecture models with their security trade-offs.

Run it

python main.py lab 20

insight.objective: SY0-701 3.1 Security implications of architecture models: cloud, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA.
concepts: Responsibility matrix: the provider always owns the physical layer; the customer always owns its data and user access.
IaaS = you patch the guest OS; PaaS = you secure your code; SaaS = you configure users and data. Serverless = no OS for you to patch.
Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and scannable: fix the template once and every copy is fixed.
Network infrastructure: air-gapped (physical isolation), logical segmentation (VLANs/subnets), SDN (central software control plane).
High availability spreads critical resources across zones; considerations trade availability and resilience against cost.
failure_modes: A public storage bucket or public database: the most common cloud data exposure.
Security groups allowing SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it was quicker to test'.
IAM policies with action '*' on resource '*' handed to CI pipelines: one leaked token = full account takeover.
Privileged or root containers sharing the host kernel, and plaintext secrets in function environment variables.
New resource types deployed without anyone reviewing them (unreviewed = unprotected).
ai_governance: An AI agent that writes IaC must pass the same policy-as-code gate as a human: the gate, not the agent, decides.
Give infrastructure agents scoped roles, never '*' on '*'; their blast radius is the permissions you grant.
Deny by default: a resource or property the agent invents that the policy does not know is blocked, not trusted.
Every finding carries its fix, so an agent can propose a remediation that a human reviews before re-running the gate.
exam_tips: 'Who patches the guest OS on IaaS?' = the customer. 'Who secures the physical data centre?' = always the provider.
ICS/SCADA, IoT and embedded systems often cannot be patched: compensate with segmentation and monitoring.
Air-gapped = physical isolation; VLAN/subnet = logical segmentation; SDN = control plane separated from data plane.
Containers share the host kernel (lighter, less isolation); VMs have their own OS on a hypervisor (VM escape, sprawl).
Microservices: smaller blast radius, larger API attack surface. RTOS: deterministic timing for real-time control.

briefing.title: Gate the 'northwind-shop-prod' cloud deployment before it ships
briefing.situation: The cloud team wants to deploy the production online shop from an infrastructure-as-code plan with 11 resources. Before it goes live, every resource must pass the security checks: no admin ports open to the internet, no public storage or databases, encryption on, and no over-powered permissions. One permission policy for the build pipeline grants full access to everything.
your_task: Scan all 11 resources in the plan against the security checks.
Record each failed check with its severity and the fix.
Deny any resource type that has no reviewed checks.
Make the deploy decision using the gate rules: any critical finding, or more high findings than allowed, blocks the release.
briefing.why_it_matters: One open admin port or public database can be found by attackers within hours. A build-pipeline account with full access means anyone who steals that pipeline can control the whole cloud account.
done_when: All 11 resources show PASS or FAIL with the checks that failed.
The gate decision is BLOCK, with the 5 critical and 3 high findings listed.
The wildcard IAM policy (iam-ci-deployer) is sent to the IAM team to be rewritten with only the actions and resources the deployer needs.

glossary.IaC (infrastructure as code): Defining servers, networks and permissions in files, so they can be reviewed before they are built.
glossary.Security group: A cloud firewall that controls which traffic can reach a resource.
glossary.IAM policy: A rule in Identity and Access Management that says which actions an account may take on which resources.
glossary.Least privilege: Giving an account only the access it needs, nothing more.
glossary.Availability zone: A separate data centre within a cloud region; using two keeps a service up if one fails.
glossary.Shared responsibility model: The split of security duties between the cloud provider and the customer.

briefing.talking_point: Scanned an 11-resource infrastructure-as-code plan, passed 3 resources and failed 8, and blocked the release on 5 critical and 3 high findings, including a build-pipeline (CI, continuous integration) deployer IAM policy that allowed every action on every resource.

labs.title: Lab 21 — Asset Inventory & Secure Disposal
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement, ownership, classification, inventory, enumeration, sanitization, destruction, certification, retention · 3.3 Data classification · 4.5 NAC
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.2 Security implications of proper hardware, software and data asset management: acquisition/procurement process; assignment/accounting (ownership, classification); monitoring/asset tracking (inventory, enumeration); disposal/decommissioning (sanitization, destruction, certification, data retention).
  • 3.3 Data classification drives the required protection (and disposal) level.
  • 4.5 Network access control (NAC) to quarantine unmanaged devices.

How it works

Part 1 — inventory reconciliation. The CMDB (what we think we own) is compared with a discovery scan (what is actually on the network), matching by MAC:

UNMANAGED     on the network but not in the CMDB (shadow IT)
MISSING       tracked as active but not seen for > missing_after_days
NO_OWNER      no accountable owner recorded
UNCLASSIFIED  no (or an unknown) data classification
OK            none of the above

Part 2 — disposal requests, NIST SP 800-88 style. Levels are ordered Clear < Purge < Destroy. The minimum level depends on classification and on whether the media is reused inside the organisation or leaves it. Each method maps to a level and to the media it works on. A request is REJECTED when the media/method/classification is unknown (deny by default), the method does not work on that media, the level is too low, a third party gives no certificate of destruction, a legal hold applies or the retention period has not expired.

Run it

python main.py lab 21

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement, assignment/accounting, tracking and disposal.
concepts: Procurement is the first control: buy through an approved process so every asset enters the inventory with an owner.
Assignment/accounting gives every asset an accountable owner and a data classification.
Monitoring/tracking compares the inventory with enumeration (discovery scans) to find unmanaged and missing assets.
NIST SP 800-88 levels: Clear (logical overwrite) < Purge (crypto-erase, secure erase, degauss) < Destroy (shred, pulverize, incinerate).
Disposal needs certification (certificate of destruction) and must respect data retention and legal holds.
failure_modes: Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data survives.
Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use crypto-erase or destroy.
Paying a shredding vendor without getting a certificate of destruction: no proof, no accountability.
Destroying records still under retention or legal hold (spoliation of evidence).
ai_governance: Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner and a classification.
An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT: onboard it or block it.
When decommissioning an AI system, sanitize its training data, vector stores, logs and backups too.
An AI asset agent may reconcile and recommend, but disposal approval stays with a human owner.
exam_tips: 'Device on the network not in the inventory' = unmanaged asset / shadow IT; NAC can quarantine it.
'SSD leaving the organisation' = crypto-erase/secure erase (purge) or physical destruction, never degauss.
Certificate of destruction = documented proof that media was destroyed, usually from a third party.
Legal hold overrides the retention schedule: nothing under hold may be deleted or destroyed.
Clear protects against simple recovery tools; Purge against laboratory recovery; Destroy makes reuse impossible.

briefing.title: Reconcile the asset inventory with the network scan and approve disposal requests
briefing.situation: Our asset records (the CMDB) list 8 devices, but a network scan found extra devices nobody registered, and one laptop has not been seen in 20 days. Some assets have no owner or no data label. Separately, nine requests to wipe or destroy old drives, tapes, USB sticks and paper are waiting for approval.
your_task: Compare the CMDB with the scan and flag missing, unowned, unclassified and unmanaged devices.
Give each finding an action, such as locate the asset, assign an owner, or quarantine with network access control.
Check each disposal request: the method must meet the needed level (clear, purge, destroy) for the media type and data label.
Reject any request under legal hold, still inside its retention period, or missing a certificate of destruction.
briefing.why_it_matters: A lost laptop or an unknown device on the network can leak data or give attackers a foothold. A drive wiped the wrong way can be recovered by whoever buys it.
done_when: Every CMDB entry and scanned device has a finding and an action.
All 9 disposal requests have a decision and a reason.
The IAM team is asked to revoke sessions and device access for the owner of missing laptop-17, and to record a named owner for print-02 and cam-lobby so every asset maps to a real person.

glossary.CMDB (configuration management database): The official record of an organization's devices and who owns them.
glossary.Shadow IT: Devices or services used without IT's approval.
glossary.NAC (network access control): Technology that checks a device before letting it onto the network.
glossary.Clear / purge / destroy: Three levels of data removal: overwrite, make unrecoverable even in a lab, or physically destroy.
glossary.Degaussing: Erasing magnetic media with a strong magnet; it does nothing to SSDs (solid-state drives).
glossary.Legal hold: An order to keep data because of a lawsuit or investigation.
glossary.Certificate of destruction: Proof from a disposal vendor that the media was really destroyed.

briefing.talking_point: Reconciled an 8-asset CMDB with a discovery scan, finding 1 missing laptop, 3 unmanaged devices, 2 assets without owners and 2 unclassified, and approved 3 of 9 disposal requests while rejecting 6, including an SSD set for degaussing and media under legal hold.

labs.title: Lab 22 — Compliance & Privacy Obligations Tracker
labs.objectives: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring, privacy (subject, controller vs processor, retention, right to be forgotten) · 5.1 Data roles: owner, controller, processor, custodian/steward
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 5.4 Effective security compliance: compliance reporting (internal, external), consequences of non-compliance (fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts), compliance monitoring (due diligence/care, attestation and acknowledgement, internal and external, automation), privacy (legal implications: local/regional, national, global; data subject; controller vs processor; ownership; data inventory and retention; right to be forgotten).
  • 5.1 Roles and responsibilities for data: owners, controllers, processors, custodians/stewards.

Model

Time is a plain integer: as_of_day (hours = day × 24). There is no real clock. Every deadline, period and margin comes from the compliance policy. The regimes ("GDPR-style" 30 days / 72 h, a fictional "state privacy law" 45 days) are configurable ILLUSTRATIONS for learning, NOT legal advice.

Each case is evaluated to one status, with reasons, a rule code, a consequence category and the reporting it needs (internal / external / none):

  • COMPLIANT obligation met, or on track with time to spare
  • AT_RISK open, and the deadline falls within the policy margin
  • NON_COMPLIANT deadline missed or a required step missing
  • EXEMPT a valid, DOCUMENTED exception (legal hold, retention duty)

Case kinds: data subject requests (access / erasure "right to be forgotten" / rectification), breach notifications, data retention, attestations. Unknown regime/type or a missing required field → NON_COMPLIANT (deny by default).

Run it

python main.py lab 22

insight.objective: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring and privacy (with 5.1 data roles).
concepts: Deadlines here are configurable illustrations (GDPR-style 30 days / 72 h), not legal advice; real law varies by local, regional, national and global scope.
The controller decides why/how data is processed and answers data subject requests; a processor acts only on its instructions.
Right to be forgotten is not absolute: a documented legal hold or retention obligation suspends erasure.
A data inventory plus a retention schedule (minimum AND maximum periods) drives lawful keeping and destruction.
Compliance monitoring: attestation and acknowledgement, internal and external audits, and automation of the checks.
failure_modes: Silently deleting data that is under legal hold (sanctions for spoliation).
Keeping data 'just in case' long after its retention period (over-retention increases breach impact).
A processor answering a subject request directly instead of forwarding it to the controller.
Missing the regulator breach notification window while the investigation drags on.
Annual policy acknowledgements tracked on paper and quietly expiring.
ai_governance: An AI agent that handles DSRs must verify identity before disclosing or erasing anything.
Agents need the data inventory too: training data and prompts are personal data with retention limits.
Exceptions (holds) must be documented records an agent can check, never a free-text excuse it accepts.
Automated compliance checks are monitoring, but attestation sign-off stays with an accountable human.
exam_tips: Internal reporting goes to management/board/compliance; external reporting goes to regulators, customers or auditors.
Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage, loss of license, contractual impacts.
Due diligence = investigate and verify; due care = act as a reasonable, prudent organisation would.
Controller vs processor: the controller is accountable; the processor processes on the controller's behalf.
Data subject = the person the data is about; right to be forgotten = erasure request.

briefing.requested_by: Helen Marsh, Privacy and Compliance Manager
briefing.title: Thirteen privacy and compliance obligations: which are late?
briefing.situation: The compliance team is tracking 13 open items as of day 1000: customer requests to see, correct or delete their data, three data breaches, data-retention cases and signed attestations. Some deadlines have already passed, and one customer request was sent to our payroll provider instead of to us. Leadership needs a status report and to know which items must be reported outside the company.
your_task: Apply each item's deadline rule and mark it COMPLIANT, AT_RISK, NON_COMPLIANT or EXEMPT.
Check data-subject requests for identity verification and correct routing between controller and processor.
Check breach notices against the 72-hour regulator deadline and whether affected people were told.
Check retention cases for data kept too long or destroyed too early, allowing for legal holds, and produce the summary report.
briefing.why_it_matters: Late breach notices and missed privacy deadlines bring fines, and an expired attestation can cost a customer contract or a license. Acting on a deletion request without verifying identity can hand someone else's data to an impostor.
done_when: All 13 items have a status, a rule and a consequence.
The report shows COMPLIANT 2, AT_RISK 2, NON_COMPLIANT 7, EXEMPT 2, and lists the 4 items needing external reporting.

DSR-5 is routed to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) team to verify the requester's identity before any erasure, and for BR-3 (credential stuffing) affected customers are notified and IAM confirms the compromised accounts were reset.

glossary.DSR (data subject request): A person's request to see, correct or delete the data a company holds about them.
glossary.Data controller: The organization that decides why and how personal data is used.
glossary.Data processor: A company that handles personal data only on the controller's instructions.
glossary.Right to be forgotten: A person's right to have their data deleted, unless a law or legal hold requires keeping it.
glossary.Retention period: The minimum and maximum time a type of record must be kept.
glossary.Attestation: A signed statement that controls are in place, often owed to customers or auditors.
glossary.Credential stuffing: Trying usernames and passwords stolen from other sites on our login page.

briefing.talking_point: Tracked 13 privacy and compliance obligations and found 7 non-compliant, including a breach notice 28 hours late, audit logs destroyed 225 days early and an erasure request with no identity verification, with 4 items needing external reporting.

labs.title: Lab 23 — Penetration Test Rules-of-Engagement Gate & Audit Planner
labs.objectives: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation, internal/external, penetration testing, reconnaissance · 4.3 Penetration testing · 5.3 Rules of engagement
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 5.5 Types and purposes of audits and assessments: attestation; internal (compliance, audit committee, self-assessments); external (regulatory, examinations, assessment, independent third-party audit); penetration testing (physical, offensive, defensive, integrated, known environment, partially known environment, unknown environment, reconnaissance: passive and active).
  • 4.3 Vulnerability identification methods: penetration testing.
  • 5.3 Third-party risk: rules of engagement.

How it works

Part 1 is a rules-of-engagement (RoE) gate, the same guard a governed AI pentest agent needs. Every planned test action is checked against the signed engagement record. Any of these gives BLOCK (all reasons are listed):

  • the engagement is unsigned, signed by a role that cannot authorise testing, lacks an emergency contact or a declared environment type, or the action day is outside the authorization validity;
  • the target is missing, not inside an in-scope CIDR/domain, or matches an out-of-scope CIDR/host (checked with the ipaddress module);
  • the technique is unknown to the catalogue, prohibited by the engagement or always prohibited by policy;
  • the action declares "passive" recon but the technique actually touches the target (active), so it cannot claim the passive exemption;
  • the hour is outside the testing window. Exception (policy switch): passive recon reads only public third-party sources, so it may run outside the window, but it still needs valid authorization and an in-scope target.

Otherwise a technique that is not explicitly allowed gives NEEDS_APPROVAL (deny by default: written approval from the signer first), else ALLOW.

Part 2 is an audit planner: each assessment need is mapped by its driver (regulator, audit committee, compliance, customer SOC 2, self-check) and its independence requirement to an assessment type. Unknown driver → UNCLASSIFIED.

Run it

python main.py lab 23

insight.objective: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation, internal/external audits, penetration testing and reconnaissance.
concepts: Rules of engagement set scope, timing, allowed and prohibited techniques, and an emergency contact; signed authorization comes first.
Known, partially known and unknown environments describe how much the testers are told beforehand.
Passive recon uses public sources (OSINT, WHOIS, certificate logs); active recon sends traffic to the target (port scans, banner grabs).
Offensive = red team, defensive = blue team, integrated = purple team; physical tests target doors, badges and guards.
Internal audits (compliance, audit committee, self-assessment) differ from external ones (regulatory exam, independent third-party audit, attestation).
failure_modes: Scanning an IP that 'looked like ours' but belonged to a neighbour: unauthorised access, whatever the intent.
Running a DoS test in business hours with no emergency contact, causing a real outage.
Treating a team's self-assessment as if it gave an independent opinion.
Calling an active scan 'passive' to slip outside the agreed testing window.
ai_governance: An AI pentest agent should call an RoE gate before every action, not once at the start of the engagement.
Deny by default: an unknown technique or an unparseable target is BLOCKED, never guessed.
The agent's own label (e.g. 'passive') is untrusted; the gate reclassifies the technique from its catalogue.
Out-of-scope lists win over in-scope ranges, and every decision is logged with its reasons for the final report.
exam_tips: 'Testers are given network diagrams and credentials' = known environment; 'given nothing' = unknown environment.
OSINT, WHOIS and social-media research = passive reconnaissance; ping sweeps and port scans = active.
Attestation = an independent party formally vouches for controls (e.g. a SOC 2 report).
Audit committee oversees internal audit; regulators perform examinations; an outside auditor gives independence.
Purple team = integrated testing where red and blue teams share findings.

briefing.title: Check ten planned pen-test actions against the signed rules of engagement
briefing.situation: Our client signed rules of engagement for a 10-day penetration test, listing the in-scope networks, the excluded ones, allowed testing hours and banned techniques. Ten test actions are planned, some by a human tester and some by an AI testing agent. The client also needs five upcoming audits matched to the right type of assessment.
your_task: Check each planned action is signed off, inside the authorized dates and inside an in-scope target range.
Check the technique is allowed and the time is inside the testing window, with the stated exemption for passive research.
Mark each action ALLOW, BLOCK or NEEDS_APPROVAL, and name who must approve.
Match each audit need to the right assessment type, and whether it is internal or external.
briefing.why_it_matters: Testing outside the signed scope or hours is unauthorized access, which can break the law and take down a client's systems. Picking the wrong kind of audit can fail a regulator or customer requirement.
done_when: All 10 actions have a decision and a reason (2 allowed, 7 blocked, 1 needing approval).
The web-app test is held until the CISO gives written approval.
All 5 assessment needs are matched to a type, and the IAM team confirms the AI agent and tester accounts are disabled after day 10.

glossary.Penetration test: An authorized, simulated attack to find weaknesses before real attackers do.
glossary.Rules of engagement (RoE): The signed agreement that sets what testers may touch, how and when.
glossary.Scope: The list of systems that may be tested; anything else is off limits.
glossary.Passive vs active reconnaissance: Passive research reads public sources only; active research sends traffic to the target.
glossary.Attestation (SOC 2): An independent auditor's report on a company's controls.
glossary.CISO: Chief information security officer, the senior security leader.

briefing.talking_point: Gated 10 planned penetration-test actions against signed rules of engagement, allowing 2, blocking 7 for scope, time window, banned or unknown technique and expired authorization, and holding 1 for CISO approval, then matched 5 audit needs to the right assessment type.

labs.title: Lab 24 — Security Awareness Program Analyzer
labs.objectives: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness: phishing campaigns, anomalous behaviour, training, reporting · 2.2 Phishing/BEC vectors
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 5.6 Implement security awareness practices: phishing (campaigns, recognizing a phishing attempt, responding to reported suspicious messages), anomalous behavior recognition (risky, unexpected, unintentional), user guidance and training (policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider threat, password management, removable media and cables, social engineering, operational security, hybrid/remote work environments), reporting and monitoring (initial, recurring), development, execution.
  • 2.2 Threat vectors: phishing, business email compromise, impersonation, typosquatting (lookalike domains).

Model

1. Phishing simulation: each employee's events give an outcome (COMPROMISED > CLICKED > REPORTED > PASSED; no delivery record → NO_DATA). The outcome maps to an action through a role-tier table (high-risk roles such as finance/exec/it_admin get a stricter table; an unknown role is treated as high-risk). Repeat offenders (prior + this failure ≥ the tier threshold) → ESCALATE_TO_MANAGER. No training record → untrained, training older than the recurring cadence → overdue (deny by default). Department rates are checked against thresholds and program KPIs vs targets. 2. Anomalous behaviour: ordered policy rules classify observations as RISKY / UNINTENTIONAL / UNEXPECTED / NOT_ANOMALOUS; a missing attribute gives the default class (RISKY) because intent cannot be ruled out. 3. Phishing indicators: weighted indicators (lookalike sender, urgency, mismatched link text vs href, credential/payment request, risky attachment) → REPORT_AS_PHISHING when the score reaches the threshold.

Run it

python main.py lab 24

insight.objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns, anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
concepts: Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission and report rates; the report rate matters most.
Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC, hybrid/remote work.
Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery, simulations) and measured against KPIs.
failure_modes: Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is your early-warning sensor.
One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually recognises a phish.
Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although BEC targets high-risk roles.
Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of untrained.
Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so evidence disappears.
ai_governance: An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one, not just say 'safe'.
Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow instructions found inside an email.
An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and insider-threat referral need a human.
Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts can be audited and contested.
exam_tips: Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable media training (baiting).
Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline, unintentional = accident: know the three words.
Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

briefing.requested_by: Natalie Brooks, Security Awareness Program Lead
briefing.title: Phishing test PH-2026-Q4 results: who clicked, who gave up a password, what next
briefing.situation: We ran a simulated phishing email for 12 employees in Finance, Engineering, Sales and HR. Two people entered their passwords on the fake page, and three clicked the link. We also have five unusual behaviour reports, like an admin stopping security software, and four real emails users forwarded for a verdict.
your_task: Give each employee a follow-up action based on their result, role risk, repeat failures and training record.
Calculate click, password-entry and report rates by department and for the whole program, against targets.
Classify the five behaviour reports and pick a response and a technical control for each.
Score the four forwarded emails on phishing signs and mark each one REPORT_AS_PHISHING or LIKELY_SAFE.
briefing.why_it_matters: A password typed into a fake page is a real account compromise until it is reset. Departments that handle money, like Finance, are the main targets for invoice and payment fraud.
done_when: All 12 employees have an action and the rule that triggered it.
Department and program metrics are reported, with Finance, HR and Sales flagged.
The two password submitters (E03, E08) are sent to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) team for a forced password reset, session revocation and a check of multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Both risky behaviours (B1, B4) are referred to the insider-threat team.

glossary.Phishing simulation: A safe, fake phishing email sent to staff to measure and train their responses.
glossary.Credential submission: Typing a username and password into the fake page; in real life, the account would be compromised.
glossary.Report rate: The share of people who reported the email to security.
glossary.BEC (business email compromise): A scam that uses fake or hijacked business email to get payments or data.
glossary.Typosquatting: Using a look-alike domain, like examp1e.com, to trick people.
glossary.UEBA: User and entity behaviour analytics: tools that flag activity unusual for a person or device.

briefing.talking_point: Analyzed a 12-person phishing test with a 41.7% click rate and 16.7% password-entry rate, flagged 3 of 4 departments, sent the 2 compromised users to IAM for forced resets and session revocation, and flagged 2 of 4 forwarded emails as phishing.

labs.title: Lab 25 — Conditional Access & Just-in-Time Privileged Access
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.6 IAM: MFA, conditional access, least privilege, PAM (JIT, vaulting, ephemeral credentials) · 1.2 Zero trust adaptive identity, policy engine/enforcement · 2.4 Impossible travel, concurrent sessions
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.6 Identity and access management: multifactor authentication, attribute-based / conditional access, least privilege, privileged access management tools (just-in-time permissions, password vaulting, ephemeral credentials).
  • 1.2 Zero trust: adaptive identity, policy-driven access control, Policy Engine (decides) and Policy Enforcement Point (enforces).
  • 2.4 Indicators of malicious activity: impossible travel, concurrent session usage.

Model

Part 1 is a Conditional Access evaluator (the same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access, written with generic names). A policy *applies* to a sign-in when its users, apps and every condition match (sign-in risk, device platform, named/trusted location, client app type). Exclusions beat inclusions. Then:

  • every applicable policy is evaluated; ANY applicable block wins → BLOCK;
  • otherwise the grant requirements of ALL applicable policies must be met (AND across policies; inside one policy "require one of" or "require all");
  • only MFA is missing → INTERRUPTED_MFA_REQUIRED (the user is prompted); any other control missing (e.g. compliant device) → BLOCK;
  • met, and MFA was one of the requirements → ALLOW_AFTER_MFA, else ALLOW;
  • report-only policies are evaluated and logged ("would have ..."), never enforced;
  • no enforced policy applies → ALLOW with a coverage-gap flag for sensitive apps, or BLOCK for apps listed in block_if_no_policy_for (deny by default).

Missing data is unsafe: unknown risk = high, unknown client app = legacy, missing device compliance / MFA / approved app / terms of use = not satisfied.

Part 2 is just-in-time privileged role activation (PIM-style). Requests are APPROVE / PENDING_APPROVAL / DENY from per-role settings (eligibility, max duration, justification, ticket, MFA on activation, approval by someone other than the requester). Permanent active admin roles are standing-privilege findings; break-glass accounts must be excluded from every policy and alerted on.

Run it

python main.py lab 25

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.6 Conditional access, MFA, least privilege, PAM (JIT) · 1.2 Adaptive identity, PE/PEP · 2.4 Impossible travel.
concepts: Conditional access is if-then policy: IF user, app, risk, device, location and client app match, THEN block or require controls.
All applicable policies are combined: any block wins, otherwise every required control from every policy must be met.
Exclusions beat inclusions; report-only mode logs what a policy would do before you enforce it.
PAM: just-in-time permissions replace standing admin roles; password vaulting and ephemeral credentials limit what can be stolen.
Same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access / PIM (SC-300), described here with generic terms.
failure_modes: Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits the moment one account is phished.
Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
Assuming 'no policy matched' means 'blocked': without a deny-by-default rule it means allowed with a password only.
Letting requesters approve their own privileged activation.
ai_governance: Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
An agent may draft activation requests, but a human approver who is not the requester must approve high-privilege roles.
Run new agent access policies in report-only mode first and review the 'would have blocked' log.
exam_tips: 'Access changes based on location, device health and risk' = conditional / context-aware access, adaptive identity.
'Admin rights granted only for the time needed, then revoked' = just-in-time permissions (PAM).
'Credentials that exist for one session' = ephemeral credentials; 'checked out from a vault' = password vaulting.
Two logins from distant countries minutes apart = impossible travel (an indicator of compromised credentials).
Policy Engine decides, Policy Enforcement Point enforces; conditional access is the policy engine for sign-ins.

briefing.requested_by: Renee Holloway, IT Audit Manager, Prairie Wind Credit Union
briefing.title: Check our sign-in rules and who holds admin rights before the identity audit
briefing.situation: Auditors want proof that our sign-in rules work and that nobody keeps admin rights they do not need. We have eight Conditional Access policies (if-then rules that decide what a sign-in needs), a log of 13 recent sign-ins, a list of who holds admin roles, and seven requests from staff to switch on an admin role for a short time. Some rules may be missing, and two people have had full admin rights for years.
your_task: Run each sign-in through every policy and record the outcome: allowed, allowed after MFA (multifactor authentication), stopped for MFA, or blocked.
Note what the report-only (test-mode) policy would have done, without enforcing it.
Flag sensitive apps that no policy protects, and suspicious patterns such as impossible travel.
Review admin role assignments: flag permanent admin rights and check the two emergency (break-glass) accounts.
Approve, hold for approval, or deny each request to switch on an admin role, using the role's rules.
briefing.why_it_matters: One stolen password on an account that always has admin rights can hand an attacker the whole company. Sign-in rules that silently miss an app, or old email protocols that skip MFA, are how most account takeovers start.
done_when: Every sign-in has an outcome and the list of policies that applied, with a reason.
Coverage gaps, impossible travel and the report-only results are written up for the auditor.
Each permanent admin assignment has a fix (make it eligible, just-in-time) and the break-glass findings are logged.
Every role activation request has a decision with the rule that drove it.

glossary.Conditional Access: If-then sign-in rules: if this user, app, location, device or risk matches, then block or require extra checks.
glossary.MFA (multifactor authentication): Proving who you are with two or more kinds of proof, such as a password plus a phone prompt.
glossary.Report-only mode: A policy that is tested and logged but not enforced, so you can see its effect before switching it on.
glossary.Legacy authentication: Old email sign-in methods (IMAP, POP, basic SMTP) that cannot ask for MFA.
glossary.Just-in-time (JIT) access: Admin rights switched on only when needed, for a few hours, then removed automatically.
glossary.Standing privilege: Admin rights that are switched on all the time, whether or not they are being used.
glossary.Break-glass account: An emergency admin account kept out of normal sign-in rules so you are never locked out, and watched closely.
glossary.Impossible travel: Two sign-ins for one person from places too far apart to travel between in the time shown.

briefing.talking_point: Evaluated 13 sign-ins against 8 Conditional Access policies (4 blocked, 3 allowed after MFA, 2 stopped for MFA), caught an impossible-travel sign-in and an unprotected payroll app, flagged 2 permanent admin assignments and a mis-configured break-glass account, and decided 7 just-in-time admin requests (2 approved, 1 sent for approval, 4 denied).

labs.title: Lab 26 — Identity Governance: Account Reconciliation & Access Certification
labs.objectives: SY0-701 4.6 Provisioning/de-provisioning, permission assignments, attestation, least privilege · 5.1 Governance roles: owners/custodians · 4.2 Inventory/enumeration of accounts
labs.lesson_html:
Security+ SY0-701 objectives

  • 4.6 Identity and access management: provisioning/de-provisioning user accounts, permission assignments and implications, attestation, least privilege, privileged access management.
  • 5.1 Security governance: roles and responsibilities for systems and data (owners, custodians/stewards), monitoring and revision.
  • 4.2 Asset management: inventory and enumeration (here, of accounts).

How it works

This is the daily work of an identity governance and administration (IGA) analyst, using the same concepts SailPoint and Entra ID Governance use.

1. Aggregation & correlation: HR is the authoritative source. Every application account is correlated to an identity by ordered policy rules (employee_id, else email, else none). Service accounts correlate to their named owner. Findings (most severe wins): TERMINATED_WITH_ACCESS, PRIVILEGED_UNOWNED, ORPHAN, DUPLICATE, DORMANT, else CORRELATED. An unknown HR status is treated as terminated and a missing login as dormant. 2. Access certification: each review item is KEEP, REVOKE or ESCALATE. Unknown or terminated identity → REVOKE. The reviewer must be the identity's manager or the entitlement owner, never the identity itself, or the item is ESCALATED. No decision at close → policy action (REVOKE). An approval escalates if it is high-risk with no comment, completes an SoD pair, or comes from a rubber-stamping reviewer (≥ N approvals with a median decision time < Y seconds).

Run it

python main.py lab 26

insight.objective: SY0-701 4.6 Provisioning/de-provisioning and attestation · 5.1 Owners · 4.2 Account inventory.
concepts: HR is the authoritative source; aggregation pulls every app's accounts, correlation links each to a person.
An entitlement is one permission; an access profile bundles one app's entitlements; a role bundles profiles for a job.
Orphaned, dormant and terminated-but-enabled accounts are de-provisioning failures an attacker can reuse.
Access certification (attestation) has the manager or entitlement owner re-approve access on a schedule.
These are the same concepts SailPoint and Entra ID Governance use, shown here with generic terms.
failure_modes: Leaver process disables the directory account but not the ERP or SaaS accounts.
Service accounts created for a project with no owner, still privileged years later.
Reviewers approving everything in seconds: the certification becomes paperwork, not a control.
Treating an undecided item as 'keep' so access survives because nobody looked at it.
ai_governance: An AI agent can aggregate and correlate accounts, but revoking access stays a human-approved, logged change.
Give an agent a service account with a named human owner and least privilege, then certify it like any other.
Agents that recommend approve/revoke must show reasons; a reviewer who just accepts them is rubber-stamping.
Treat comments and attributes in app exports as untrusted data, never as instructions to the agent.
exam_tips: 'Account still active after the employee left' = de-provisioning failure; fix with HR-driven automation.
'Periodic review where managers confirm access' = attestation / access recertification.
Least privilege: when a reviewer does not respond, remove the access (deny by default).
Data/system owner decides who gets access; the custodian implements it.

briefing.title: Clean up accounts in ERP, CRM and FileShare before the Q4 access review closes
briefing.situation: Internal audit found that Redbud Example Co cannot prove who owns every login in its three main applications: the ERP (finance system), the CRM (customer system) and FileShare. HR has exported its list of 10 people, and each app has exported its accounts, 25 in total. At the same time, managers have just finished the quarterly access review, and audit thinks some of them clicked 'approve' without reading.
your_task: Match every app account to a person in the HR list, by employee ID first and by email if there is no ID.
Flag accounts nobody owns, accounts of people who have left, unused accounts, extra accounts and service accounts without an owner.
Check each review decision: was the reviewer allowed to decide, was a reason given for risky access, and does the approval break a separation-of-duties rule?
Spot reviewers who approved everything too fast, and remove access that nobody decided on.
Hand the app teams one de-provisioning list of accounts and permissions to remove.
briefing.why_it_matters: A login that belongs to nobody, or to someone who has left, is an open door for an attacker and a failed audit. An access review that people rubber-stamp gives false comfort and will not satisfy auditors.
done_when: All 25 accounts have a finding and an action, and every flagged account has a written reason.
Every review item is marked KEEP, REVOKE or ESCALATE with the reason.
The reviewer who rubber-stamped is named, and completion and revocation rates are reported.
The de-provisioning list is ready for the application owners.

glossary.Identity governance and administration (: The practice and tools that track who has which access, why they have it, and whether they still need it.
glossary.Authoritative source: The system of record for who works here, usually HR, which decides whether a person exists and is active.
glossary.Correlation: Linking each application account to the person who owns it, using matching rules such as employee ID or email.
glossary.Orphaned account: An account that no current person in HR owns, so nobody is accountable for it.
glossary.Entitlement: One specific permission inside an application, such as 'approve payments'.
glossary.Access certification (attestation): A regular review where a manager or the permission's owner confirms that each person still needs their access.
glossary.Separation of duties (SoD): A rule that one person must not hold two powers that together allow fraud, such as creating a supplier and paying it.

briefing.talking_point: Reconciled 25 accounts across 3 applications against HR, flagging 13 for action (2 leavers with live access, 3 orphans, 3 unowned privileged accounts, 3 dormant and 2 duplicates), and certified 16 review items: kept 3, revoked 4 and escalated 9, including a separation-of-duties conflict (supplier creation plus payment approval), a self-review and a reviewer who approved 5 items at a median of 4 seconds each.

career_tracks._note: How the labs map to an Identity & Access Management (IAM) career path. Skill-area names follow the public outlines of each certification/platform; the mapping to labs is this project's own and describes simulated practice, not vendor training.

path.name: CompTIA Security+ (SY0-701)
path.why: The baseline security certification most IAM job postings ask for; covers identity, access control, zero trust and governance alongside the rest of security.

path.name: Microsoft SC-300: Identity and Access Administrator
path.why: Shows you can run identity in Microsoft Entra ID, the identity platform behind Microsoft 365 and Azure that most organisations use.

path.name: SailPoint identity governance (IdentityIQ / Identity Security Cloud)
path.why: SailPoint is a leading identity governance (IGA) product; employers that run it hire analysts and engineers who understand lifecycle, certifications and SoD.

areas.name: Implement and manage user identities
areas.plain: Create and manage users and groups, invite guests from other companies, and keep on-premises and cloud accounts in sync.

areas.name: Implement authentication and access management
areas.plain: Decide how people sign in (MFA, passwordless) and write the rules that allow, challenge or block a sign-in (Conditional Access, risk-based policies).

areas.name: Plan and implement workload identities
areas.plain: Govern the non-human identities: app registrations, service principals, managed identities and the permissions apps and automations get.

areas.name: Plan and automate identity governance
areas.plain: Keep access right over time: access packages, access reviews, just-in-time admin roles (PIM), and monitoring sign-in and audit logs.

areas.name: Identity lifecycle (joiner, mover, leaver)
areas.plain: Give new hires the right access on day one, adjust it when they change jobs, and remove all of it when they leave.

areas.name: Aggregation and correlation
areas.plain: Pull every account from every application and match each one to a person from the HR system; unmatched accounts are orphans.

areas.name: Roles, access profiles and entitlements
areas.plain: Bundle permissions into roles so access is granted by job, not one permission at a time.

areas.name: Access certifications (reviews)
areas.plain: Managers and owners regularly confirm or revoke each person's access, with evidence for auditors.

areas.name: Separation-of-duties (SoD) policies
areas.plain: Stop one person from holding two permissions that together allow fraud, such as creating and approving a payment.

areas.name: Provisioning, access requests and approvals
areas.plain: Grant and remove access through requests, approvals and automation instead of manual admin work.

areas.name: Audit evidence and reporting
areas.plain: Show auditors who had access, who approved it, and when it was removed.

areas.name: 4.6 Identity and access management
areas.plain: Provisioning, SSO and federation, access-control models, MFA, passwords and privileged access management.

areas.name: 1.2 Zero trust and AAA
areas.plain: Never trust by default: verify every request using identity, device and context.

areas.name: 5.1 Governance and data roles
areas.plain: Owners, custodians and policies that decide who may approve access.

areas.name: 4.7 Automation and orchestration
areas.plain: Automating provisioning and response safely, with guard rails and human approval.

job_search: Search the titles above plus the words SailPoint, Entra ID, Azure AD, Okta, CyberArk and access reviews; many IAM roles are hybrid or fully remote, which widens an Oklahoma search.

In Oklahoma, look at the state's central IT agency job board, large hospital systems, energy companies, banks and credit unions, aerospace and defense employers around Tinker Air Force Base, universities, and tribal nations and their enterprises, all of which run identity programs.
Read five real postings and copy their keywords into your resume and portfolio captions; match each keyword to a lab you can show.
Be explicit that portfolio work is a simulated lab with fictional data; interviewers value honest, well-explained practice over vague claims.
portfolio_guide: For each lab, capture four things: the work ticket (Lesson tab), the scenario run (Run the scenario tab), the case study page (Case study tab, Print / Save as PDF), and your practice score.
Screenshots: Windows Snipping Tool (Win+Shift+S) or macOS (Shift+Cmd+4). Screen recordings: Windows Game Bar (Win+G), macOS (Shift+Cmd+5) or the free OBS Studio.

Record a 60-90 second walkthrough per lab: the ticket and why it matters, run the scenario, point at two findings, say what you would fix, end with the lesson. Talk to the camera like you are briefing your team lead.
Publish the case-study Markdown files (python main.py case-study --all) in a GitHub repository with your screenshots, and post one lab a week on LinkedIn using the talking point.
Lead with the IAM labs (1, 2, 25, 26, then 5 and 8) when applying for identity roles.

|    Transfer mailbox + file ownership to manager
|    Recover badge, laptop and mobile device
|    Retain account (disabled) for legal-hold period, then delete

User   Action             Resource          Decision  Gate    Reason

u1004  hr_records:read    salary-band-2026  DENY      RBAC    no role grants 'hr_records:read'
u1003  deploy:production  payroll-app       ALLOW     ALLOW   all gates passed
