case_study.title: Threat Actor & Attack Vector Classifier
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 2.1 Threat actors & motivations · 2.2 Threat vectors · 2.5 Mitigations

briefing.title: Classify eight open cases by who attacked, why, and how they got in
briefing.situation: The security team has eight open cases, from a quiet data theft at a defense contractor to USB sticks left in a parking lot. Each case lists clues an analyst already gathered, such as 'demands payment' or 'used a valid account'. Leadership wants every case labelled with the type of attacker, their motive, and the way they got in, so the right fix goes to the right place.
your_task: Score each case's clues against the known attacker profiles (nation-state, organized crime, hacktivist, insider, unskilled attacker, shadow IT) and pick the best match.
Map the strongest clue to a motive, such as espionage, financial gain, revenge or blackmail.
Record the initial access vector (the way in), such as phishing email, default password or a phone call to the help desk.
List one fix for the way in, plus one extra control suited to that type of attacker.
briefing.why_it_matters: If you blame everything on a foreign government, you overspend and miss the simple holes, like default passwords. If you fix the malware but not the way it got in, the attacker walks back in next week.
done_when: All 8 cases have an attacker type, a motive and an entry vector, with the clues and scores that support each one.
Each case lists a fix for its entry vector and a control matched to the attacker.
The insider case (T-04) and the help-desk phone scam (T-08) are handed to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) team for access review and reset-procedure fixes.

glossary.Threat actor: The person or group behind an attack, such as a criminal gang or a disgruntled employee.
glossary.Nation-state / APT: A government-backed attacker; APT means advanced persistent threat, a well-funded attacker who stays hidden for a long time.
glossary.Hacktivist: An attacker who acts to promote a political or social cause.
glossary.Insider threat: A risk from someone who already has legitimate access, like an employee or contractor.
glossary.Shadow IT: Apps or services staff use without IT's approval, often with no bad intent.
glossary.Threat vector: The route an attacker uses to get in, such as email, a USB drive or a phone call.
glossary.Vishing: Voice phishing: tricking someone over the phone, for example into resetting a password.

briefing.talking_point: Classified 8 incidents by threat actor, motive and entry vector: 3 organized crime, 1 nation-state, 1 hacktivist, 1 insider, 1 unskilled attacker and 1 shadow IT case, and sent the insider and help-desk vishing cases to IAM for access and reset-process fixes.

lessons: Attributing every incident to a nation-state: it inflates the response and hides basic hygiene gaps.
Ignoring shadow IT because 'nobody was malicious' when the data exposure is just as real.
Treating insiders like outsiders: perimeter controls do nothing against valid credentials.
governance: An AI threat-intel agent should output 'Undetermined' rather than guess attribution; attribution errors drive bad decisions.
Require agents to list the indicators behind every classification so analysts can challenge them.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

--- Step 1 — Achieved vs target (as of 2026-11-03) --------------------------

Recovery capability
System        Target RTO/RPO  Host fail RTO/RPO  Site loss RTO/RPO                        Restore  Verdict
------------  --------------  -----------------  ---------------------------------------  -------  -------
payroll-app   8h / 4h         8.5h / 24h         172.5h / 24h                             4.5h     GAPS
web-frontend  1h / 24h        0h / 15m           1h / 15m                                 18m      MEETS_TARGETS
auth-service  1h / 15m        15m / 15m          1h / 15m                                 22.8m    GAPS
erp-legacy    4h / 1h         15.25h / 24h       ∞ (cannot recover) / ∞ (cannot recover)  11.25h   GAPS
file-server   24h / 24h       5.5h / 24h         not required                             1.5h     MEETS_TARGETS

--- Step 2 — Gaps and cheapest fixes ----------------------------------------
payroll-app — GAPS
  • RTO: host failure takes 8.5h (rebuild + differential restore) > target 8h
  • RPO: up to 24h of data lost > target 4h
  • SITE: cold site recovery takes 172.5h > target 8h
  • SITE RPO: after a site loss up to 24h of data is lost > target 4h
  • TEST: DR failover last tested 2025-01-10 (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Add active-passive clustering (failover 15m, $30,000/yr)
  • → Back up at least every 4h (snapshots/journaling between full backups)
  • → Use a hot site (ready in 1h, $500,000/yr)
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
web-frontend — MEETS_TARGETS
  • All targets met and tested.
auth-service — GAPS
  • DISK: RAID0 tolerates 0 disk failure(s) < required 1
  • POWER: UPS + generator run 10.2m < required 4h
  • → Rebuild storage as RAID5 (tolerates 1, 75% usable capacity)
  • → Add a generator (a UPS only bridges minutes)
erp-legacy — GAPS
  • RTO: host failure takes 15.25h (rebuild + incremental restore) > target 4h
  • RPO: up to 24h of data lost > target 1h
  • SITE: no offsite copy of the data (no replication, backups kept onsite)
  • SITE: no recovery site, so nowhere to restore to after a site loss
  • TEST: backup restore never tested (untested plan = no plan)
  • TEST: DR failover never tested (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Add active-passive clustering (failover 15m, $30,000/yr)
  • → Back up at least every 1h (snapshots/journaling between full backups)
  • → Keep an offsite/cloud backup copy (3-2-1) or replicate to the recovery site
  • → Contract a hot site
  • → Schedule a restore test and record the measured RTO/RPO
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
file-server — MEETS_TARGETS
  • All targets met and tested.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery: sites, replication, backups,
| high availability, power, testing.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • RPO is answered by backup frequency or replication; RTO by failover
| (clustering) or how fast a site can take over.
|   • Hot = running and synced (expensive); warm = hardware ready, restore
| data; cold = space and power only.
|   • Incremental backups are fastest to take but slowest to restore;
| differential is in between; full restores fastest.
|   • RAID is availability, not backup: RAID1/5/10 survive one disk, RAID6
| survives two, RAID0 survives none.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4
| hours of data.
|   • Backups stored in the same building that floods.
|   • A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
|   • A DR plan never tested; the first failover is during the real
| disaster.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for
| pre-approved, tested runbooks.
|   • Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a
| protected control (Lab 5).
|   • Use agents to run and record restore tests continuously, turning
| 'untested' into measured RTO/RPO.
|   • Declaring a disaster (moving to the alternate site) stays a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Load balancing spreads load across active nodes; clustering adds
| failover. Both are high availability.
|   • Geographic dispersion protects against regional disasters; multi-cloud
| protects against provider failure.
|   • Testing types: tabletop (discussion), simulation, fail over, parallel
| processing (run both systems).
|   • UPS = short-term power + clean shutdown; generator = long-term power.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 1 — Achieved vs target (as of 2026-11-03) --------------------------

Recovery capability
System        Target RTO/RPO  Host fail RTO/RPO  Site loss RTO/RPO                        Restore  Verdict
------------  --------------  -----------------  ---------------------------------------  -------  -------
erp-legacy    4h / 15m        5.88h / 0h         not required                             1.88h    GAPS

auth-service  24h / 1h        15m / 24h          ∞ (cannot recover) / ∞ (cannot recover)  13.8m    GAPS

--- Step 2 — Gaps and cheapest fixes ----------------------------------------
erp-legacy — GAPS
  • RTO: host failure takes 5.88h (rebuild + incremental restore) > target 4h
  • DISK: RAID10 tolerates 1 disk failure(s) < required 2
  • POWER: UPS + generator run 30m < required 8h
  • → Add active-passive clustering (failover 15m, $30,000/yr)
  • → Rebuild storage as RAID6 (tolerates 2, 67% usable capacity)
  • → Add a generator (a UPS only bridges minutes)
web-frontend — GAPS
  • RPO: up to 4h of data lost > target 1h
  • DISK: RAID1 tolerates 1 disk failure(s) < required 2
  • POWER: UPS + generator run 0h < required 1h
  • TEST: backup restore last tested 2025-06-21 (untested plan = no plan)
  • TEST: DR failover last tested 2025-03-13 (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Back up at least every 1h (snapshots/journaling between full backups)
  • → Rebuild storage as RAID6 (tolerates 2, 67% usable capacity)
  • → Add a generator (a UPS only bridges minutes)
  • → Schedule a restore test and record the measured RTO/RPO
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
db-oracle — GAPS
  • RPO: up to 12h of data lost > target 15m
  • SITE RPO: after a site loss up to 12h of data is lost > target 15m
  • TEST: DR failover never tested (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Add asynchronous replication (RPO 15m, $40,000/yr)
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
auth-service — GAPS
  • RPO: up to 24h of data lost > target 1h
  • SITE: no offsite copy of the data (no replication, backups kept onsite)
  • POWER: UPS + generator run 0h < required 4h
  • TEST: backup restore never tested (untested plan = no plan)
  • TEST: DR failover last tested 2025-03-13 (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Back up at least every 1h (snapshots/journaling between full backups)
  • → Keep an offsite/cloud backup copy (3-2-1) or replicate to the recovery site
  • → Add a generator (a UPS only bridges minutes)
  • → Schedule a restore test and record the measured RTO/RPO
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery: sites, replication, backups,
| high availability, power, testing.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • RPO is answered by backup frequency or replication; RTO by failover
| (clustering) or how fast a site can take over.
|   • Hot = running and synced (expensive); warm = hardware ready, restore
| data; cold = space and power only.
|   • Incremental backups are fastest to take but slowest to restore;
| differential is in between; full restores fastest.
|   • RAID is availability, not backup: RAID1/5/10 survive one disk, RAID6
| survives two, RAID0 survives none.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4
| hours of data.
|   • Backups stored in the same building that floods.
|   • A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
|   • A DR plan never tested; the first failover is during the real
| disaster.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for
| pre-approved, tested runbooks.
|   • Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a
| protected control (Lab 5).
|   • Use agents to run and record restore tests continuously, turning
| 'untested' into measured RTO/RPO.
|   • Declaring a disaster (moving to the alternate site) stays a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Load balancing spreads load across active nodes; clustering adds
| failover. Both are high availability.
|   • Geographic dispersion protects against regional disasters; multi-cloud
| protects against provider failure.
|   • Testing types: tabletop (discussion), simulation, fail over, parallel
| processing (run both systems).
|   • UPS = short-term power + clean shutdown; generator = long-term power.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Resilience & Recovery Planner
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery (sites, replication, backups, RAID, power, testing)

briefing.title: Can five key systems actually recover in time? Prove it before the audit
briefing.situation: The business has set recovery targets for five systems: how fast each must be back up and how much recent data it may lose. Nobody has checked those targets against what is really in place, like backup schedules, standby sites, disk setup and backup power. The auditors want proof as of 2026-11-03, including the sign-in service that every employee depends on.
your_task: Work out how long each system really takes to recover, and how much data it would lose, if a server fails and if the whole site is lost.
Compare those numbers with the business targets and mark each system MEETS_TARGETS or GAPS.
Check disk redundancy (RAID), backup power and when recovery was last tested.
Recommend the cheapest fix for each gap and note its yearly cost where the policy gives one.
briefing.why_it_matters: A plan that has never been tested usually fails during the real disaster. If the sign-in service goes down, nobody can log in to anything, so an outage there becomes an outage everywhere.
done_when: All 5 systems show achieved vs target recovery time and data loss, with a verdict.
Every gap has a specific fix, such as a hot site, more frequent backups or a generator.
The auth-service gaps (RAID0 disk with no tolerance for a failure, and 10.2 minutes of backup power against 4 hours required) are logged with the IAM platform owner.

glossary.RTO (recovery time objective): The longest a system is allowed to be down.
glossary.RPO (recovery point objective): The most recent data the business can afford to lose, measured in time.
glossary.Hot / warm / cold site: Backup locations that are fully running, partly ready, or just empty space with power.
glossary.RAID: A way of combining disks so the system keeps running if a disk fails; RAID0 survives no failures.
glossary.UPS: Uninterruptible power supply: a battery that covers minutes, not hours, until a generator starts.
glossary.Failover test: A planned drill that switches to the backup system to prove it works.

briefing.talking_point: Assessed recovery for 5 systems against business targets: 2 met, 3 had 13 gaps between them, including a legacy enterprise resource planning (ERP) system with no offsite copy and an untested plan, and a sign-in service on RAID0 with 10 minutes of backup power against a 4-hour requirement.

lessons: Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4 hours of data.
Backups stored in the same building that floods.
A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
governance: An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for pre-approved, tested runbooks.
Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a protected control (Lab 5).
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

case_study.title: Third-Party / Vendor Risk Assessor
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 5.3 Third-party risk: assessment, selection, agreements, monitoring

briefing.title: Risk-score five vendors before contracts are signed
briefing.situation: Procurement has five vendors waiting for approval, including a payroll provider, an air-conditioning contractor and a managed IT provider that wants administrator access. Each vendor filled in a security questionnaire, and legal shared the contract clauses actually signed. We need a decision on each vendor before anyone gets access to our data or network.
your_task: Score each vendor's inherent risk from what it will touch: data sensitivity, type of access, and how critical the service is.
Reduce that score by how well the vendor's questionnaire answers show working controls, giving residual risk.
Check the contract for required clauses, such as right-to-audit, breach-notice time and uptime promises.
Decide APPROVE, APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS or REJECT, and set how often each vendor is reviewed.
briefing.why_it_matters: Many large breaches start at a supplier, not at the company itself. A vendor with administrator access and an undisclosed conflict of interest is a direct path into our network.
done_when: All 5 vendors have inherent and residual risk scores and a decision.
Every missing clause or questionnaire gap is listed as a condition.
The Identity and Access Management (IAM) team confirms no vendor account or privileged access is created for a rejected vendor (VN-3, VN-5).

glossary.Inherent risk: The risk before any controls are counted.
glossary.Residual risk: The risk left after the vendor's controls are taken into account.
glossary.SOC 2 / ISO 27001: Independent audits that show a company's security controls really work.
glossary.Right-to-audit clause: Contract wording that lets us inspect the vendor's security ourselves.
glossary.SLA (service level agreement): A contract promise about uptime and response times.
glossary.MOU vs BPA: An MOU (memorandum of understanding) states intent and is usually not binding; a BPA (business partners agreement) sets binding partner duties.

briefing.talking_point: Assessed 5 vendors on inherent and residual risk: approved 1, approved 2 with conditions, and rejected 2, including a managed IT provider seeking privileged access that had not disclosed a conflict of interest.

lessons: Giving an HVAC contractor network access with no security requirements (how the 2013 Target breach began).
Signing a non-binding MOU where a binding agreement (BPA/MSA) was needed.
No right-to-audit and no independent assessment: you are trusting a marketing slide.
governance: AI vendors are third parties too: assess model providers for data use, retention, subprocessors and audit rights.
An AI procurement assistant can pre-score questionnaires, but approval and contract sign-off are human decisions.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.1 Control categories (technical, managerial,
| operational, physical) and types.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • CATEGORY = who/what implements it: technology (technical), people
| management and policy (managerial), people doing it (operational), the
| physical world (physical).
|   • TYPE = what it does: prevent, deter, detect, correct, compensate for
| another control, or direct behaviour.
|   • Every control has BOTH: a door lock is physical + preventive; a log
| review by managers is managerial + detective.
|   • Compensating controls stand in when the primary control cannot be used
| (unpatchable server → isolate it).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Only buying preventive controls; nothing detects or corrects when
| prevention fails.
|   • Writing policies (directive) with no technical enforcement or
| monitoring behind them.
|   • Calling a compensating control 'temporary' and never removing the
| underlying gap.
|   • Mapping controls inconsistently, so audits find gaps that were only
| labelling errors.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI GRC assistant can draft control mappings, but must show the
| evidence (phrases) behind each label.
|   • Ambiguous controls should come back 'Unclassified' for a human, not be
| forced into a category.
|   • AI agents themselves need controls of every type: preventive (allow-
| lists), detective (ledger), corrective (kill switch).
|   • Policy statements for agents are directive; enforce them technically
| (Lab 5) or they are only wishes.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Signs: 'Authorized personnel only' = directive; 'trespassers will be
| prosecuted' = deterrent.
|   • Backups/restore = corrective; logs/alarms/motion detectors =
| detective; firewall/locks = preventive.
|   • Guards on patrol = operational (people performing the control).
|   • Separation of duties is managerial; used in place of a missing control
| it becomes compensating.

case_study.title: Security Control Classifier (category × type)
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 1.1 Security control categories and types

briefing.title: Tag the 19 controls in our control library by category and type
briefing.situation: Our control library lists 19 security measures in plain sentences, from firewall rules to door locks to a weekly manager review of login reports. Auditors want each one tagged two ways: what kind of control it is, and what job it does. One entry is just a note about our cloud platform and may not be a control at all.
your_task: Read each control description and match key phrases to a category: technical, physical, managerial or operational.
Match key phrases to a type: preventive, deterrent, detective, corrective, compensating or directive.
Leave any entry with no matching phrases as Unclassified for a person to review.
Compare your tags with the answer key and record the score.
briefing.why_it_matters: Auditors check that every risk has controls that prevent, detect and correct problems. A library with wrong labels hides gaps, such as having lots of detection but nothing that fixes the damage afterward.
done_when: All 19 controls are tagged with a category and type, with the phrases that support each tag.
Entries with no supporting evidence are marked Unclassified instead of guessed.
Tags match the answer key, and identity controls (such as login logging and the weekly login report review) are listed for the IAM team's access review evidence.

glossary.Control category: Who or what carries out the control: technology, a physical object, management policy, or people following a procedure.
glossary.Preventive control: Stops a problem before it happens, like a door lock.
glossary.Detective control: Spots a problem while or after it happens, like a log or motion sensor.
glossary.Corrective control: Fixes the damage after a problem, like restoring from backup.
glossary.Compensating control: A substitute used when the normal control is not possible.
glossary.Directive control: Tells people what they must or must not do, like a policy or sign.

briefing.talking_point: Classified 19 security controls by category and type with 19/19 agreement with the answer key, and left the one entry with no supporting evidence as Unclassified for human review instead of guessing.

lessons: Only buying preventive controls; nothing detects or corrects when prevention fails.
Writing policies (directive) with no technical enforcement or monitoring behind them.
Calling a compensating control 'temporary' and never removing the underlying gap.
governance: An AI GRC assistant can draft control mappings, but must show the evidence (phrases) behind each label.
Ambiguous controls should come back 'Unclassified' for a human, not be forced into a category.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

--- Step 2 — Why, and how to fix it -----------------------------------------
P-01 Healthy e-commerce site → TRUSTED
  • Valid chain, name, strength, usage and revocation status.
P-02 API certificate nobody renewed → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR EXPIRED: 'api.delzarsolutions.com' expired on 2026-10-31
  • Fix: Renew and automate renewal (ACME); monitor expiry dates.
P-03 Wildcard stretched one level too far → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR HOSTNAME_MISMATCH: 'dev.portal.delzarsolutions.com' is not covered by ['*.delzarsolutions.com', 'delzarsolutions.com']
  • Fix: Re-issue with the correct SAN entries (a wildcard covers only one label).
P-04 Server forgot to send its intermediate → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR INCOMPLETE_CHAIN: issuer 'GlobalTrust TLS CA 3' was not sent and is not a trusted root (missing intermediate)
  • Fix: Configure the server to send the full chain (leaf + intermediates).
P-05 Self-signed admin console → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR SELF_SIGNED: 'admin.internal' is self-signed and not in the trust store
  • WARNING VALIDITY_TOO_LONG: leaf is valid for 3652 days (> 398)
  • WARNING REVOCATION_UNKNOWN: no OCSP answer and no CRL for the leaf; status cannot be confirmed
  • Fix: Issue the certificate from your internal CA (or a public CA); don't train users to click through warnings.
P-06 Certificate revoked after key compromise → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR REVOKED: 'vpn.delzarsolutions.com' (serial 1006) is revoked (CRL from Delzar Issuing CA 1)
  • Fix: Replace the certificate now; it was revoked (often key compromise). Investigate the key.
P-07 Legacy appliance with old crypto → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR WEAK_KEY: 'printer.delzarsolutions.com' uses RSA-1024 (< 2048)
  • ERROR WEAK_SIGNATURE: 'printer.delzarsolutions.com' is signed with sha1WithRSAEncryption
  • Fix: Generate a new key pair (RSA ≥ 2048 or EC P-256+) and a new CSR.
P-08 Mobile banking app behind a TLS-inspection proxy → UNTRUSTED
  • WARNING EXPIRING_SOON: leaf expires in 28 days (2026-12-01)
  • ERROR PIN_MISMATCH: presented key 0dd1e57ab1e5… is not one of the app's pinned keys
  • Fix: Treat as interception: verify the network path / proxy; never disable the pin to 'make it work'.
P-09 Renewal due, revocation server unreachable → TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS
  • WARNING EXPIRING_SOON: leaf expires in 17 days (2026-11-20)
  • WARNING REVOCATION_UNKNOWN: no OCSP answer and no CRL for the leaf; status cannot be confirmed
  • Fix: Enable OCSP stapling so clients always get a fresh revocation status.
P-10 A leaf certificate used to sign another → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR NOT_A_CA: 'shop.delzarsolutions.com' signed 'store.delzarsolutions.com' but is not a CA (basicConstraints CA:FALSE)
  • Fix: Re-issue from a real CA: a leaf certificate (CA:FALSE) cannot sign other certificates.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.

Connections
ID    Hostname                 Chain                                     Verdict                Primary problem
----  -----------------------  ----------------------------------------  ---------------------  ---------------
P-01  vpn.example.org          vpn.example.org → Delzar Issuing CA 1     TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS  VALIDITY_TOO_LONG
P-02  api.delzarsolutions.com  api.delzarsolutions.com → Delzar Issuing  UNTRUSTED              WEAK_SIGNATURE
P-03  api.delzarsolutions.com  api.delzarsolutions.com                   UNTRUSTED              INCOMPLETE_CHAIN
P-04  dev.portal.example.org   www.example.org                           UNTRUSTED              SELF_SIGNED
P-05  shop.example.org         shop.example.org → Delzar Issuing CA 1    UNTRUSTED              EXPIRED

--- Step 2 — Why, and how to fix it -----------------------------------------
P-01 Generated connection → TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS
  • WARNING VALIDITY_TOO_LONG: leaf is valid for 600 days (> 398)
  • Fix: Public TLS certificates are limited to 398 days; shorter lifetimes limit exposure.
P-02 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR WEAK_SIGNATURE: 'api.delzarsolutions.com' is signed with sha1WithRSAEncryption
  • Fix: Re-issue with a SHA-256 or stronger signature; SHA-1/MD5 are broken.
P-03 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR INCOMPLETE_CHAIN: issuer 'Delzar Issuing CA 1' was not sent and is not a trusted root (missing intermediate)
  • Fix: Configure the server to send the full chain (leaf + intermediates).
P-04 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR SELF_SIGNED: 'www.example.org' is self-signed and not in the trust store
  • ERROR HOSTNAME_MISMATCH: 'dev.portal.example.org' is not covered by ['www.example.org', '*.example.org']
  • Fix: Issue the certificate from your internal CA (or a public CA); don't train users to click through warnings.
P-05 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR EXPIRED: 'shop.example.org' expired on 2026-11-01
  • WARNING REVOCATION_UNKNOWN: no OCSP answer and no CRL for the leaf; status cannot be confirmed
  • Fix: Renew and automate renewal (ACME); monitor expiry dates.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 2 — Why, and how to fix it -----------------------------------------
P-01 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR PIN_MISMATCH: presented key 2f5f44792d1b… is not one of the app's pinned keys
  • Fix: Treat as interception: verify the network path / proxy; never disable the pin to 'make it work'.
P-02 Generated connection → TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS
  • WARNING REVOCATION_UNKNOWN: no OCSP answer and no CRL for the leaf; status cannot be confirmed
  • Fix: Enable OCSP stapling so clients always get a fresh revocation status.
P-03 Generated connection → TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS
  • WARNING VALIDITY_TOO_LONG: leaf is valid for 600 days (> 398)
  • Fix: Public TLS certificates are limited to 398 days; shorter lifetimes limit exposure.
P-04 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR WEAK_KEY: 'shop.example.org' uses RSA-1024 (< 2048)
  • ERROR PIN_MISMATCH: presented key a14284106862… is not one of the app's pinned keys
  • Fix: Treat as interception: verify the network path / proxy; never disable the pin to 'make it work'.
P-05 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR NOT_YET_VALID: 'mail.example.org' is not valid until 2026-11-08
  • ERROR WEAK_SIGNATURE: 'mail.example.org' is signed with md5WithRSAEncryption
  • Fix: Check the server clock / NTP and the certificate's notBefore date.
P-06 Generated connection → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR REVOKED: 'vpn.example.org' (serial 3006) is revoked (CRL from Delzar Issuing CA 1)
  • Fix: Replace the certificate now; it was revoked (often key compromise). Investigate the key.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  • Fix: Request a certificate with the serverAuth extended key usage.

  • Fix: Public TLS certificates are limited to 398 days; shorter lifetimes limit exposure.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: PKI & Certificate Validator
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 1.4 PKI: CAs, chains, CRL/OCSP, wildcard/SAN, self-signed, key length, pinning

briefing.title: Browsers and apps are showing certificate warnings on our sites
briefing.situation: Users report security warnings on several of our websites, the VPN (virtual private network) and the mobile banking app. We collected the certificate each server presented on ten connections, plus the revocation lists we could reach, as of 2026-11-03. We need to know which connections are safe and what is wrong with each of the others.
your_task: Check each connection's certificate chain back to a trusted root certificate authority.
Check expiry dates, whether the name matches the site, key strength and signature type.
Check revocation status with the CRL or OCSP, and check the mobile app's pinned keys.
Give each connection a verdict and a specific fix.
briefing.why_it_matters: An expired or revoked certificate can take an API (application programming interface) or the VPN offline, and a pin mismatch can mean someone is intercepting traffic. Teaching users to click through warnings makes real attacks easy.
done_when: All 10 connections have a verdict: TRUSTED, TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS or UNTRUSTED.
Each problem has a named fix, such as renewing, re-issuing with the right names, or sending the full chain.
The revoked VPN certificate (P-06) is escalated as a possible key compromise, and IAM is told so certificate-based sign-in to the VPN can be checked.

glossary.PKI (public key infrastructure): The system of certificates and authorities that proves a website or device is who it claims to be.
glossary.Certificate authority (CA): A trusted organization that issues and signs certificates.
glossary.Certificate chain: The links from a site's certificate up through intermediates to a trusted root.
glossary.Revocation (CRL / OCSP): Cancelling a certificate early; a CRL (certificate revocation list) or OCSP (online certificate status protocol) is how clients check.
glossary.Wildcard / SAN: Ways one certificate covers several names; a wildcard covers only one level of subdomain.
glossary.Certificate pinning: An app accepts only specific keys, so a swapped-in certificate is rejected.

briefing.talking_point: Validated 10 TLS (encrypted web) connections: 1 trusted, 1 trusted with warnings and 8 untrusted, finding an expired API certificate, a revoked VPN certificate, an overstretched wildcard, a missing intermediate, a self-signed console, weak RSA-1024 crypto, a leaf certificate misused as a CA and a pin mismatch that pointed to interception.

lessons: Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings, which makes MITM attacks invisible.
Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a revoked certificate look fine.
governance: Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be configured with 'verify=False'.
An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.

| PII must not reach an external model.

| block or quarantine transfers.

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.

| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
|

|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.

|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.

| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.

| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.

--- Step 1 — Detect and classify --------------------------------------------

Content inspection
Flow  Declared    Detections                                Effective

--- Step 2 — DLP decision per outbound flow ---------------------------------

Flows
Flow  State       Destination      Protection                            Decision
----  ----------  ---------------  ------------------------------------  --------
DF-1  in_transit  internal_app@us  tokenization + TLS channel            ALLOW
DF-2  in_use      analytics@us     masking + permission_restrictions     BLOCK
DF-3  in_transit  internal_app@us  masking + tokenization + TLS channel  ALLOW
DF-4  in_use      internal_app@us  tokenization + encryption             ALLOW
DF-5  at_rest     internal_app@eu  none                                  BLOCK
  DF-1 generated flow (health)                   ALLOW  restricted
  • content found (medical record number (PHI)) raises the label from public to restricted
  • restricted data to an approved internal_app in us; protection meets policy
  DF-2 generated flow (password)                 BLOCK  critical
  • content found (password) raises the label from public to critical
  • critical data may not go to a 'analytics' destination
  DF-3 generated flow (legal)                    ALLOW  confidential
  • content found (privileged legal material) raises the label from private to confidential
  • confidential data to an approved internal_app in us; protection meets policy
  DF-4 generated flow (email)                    ALLOW  restricted
  • restricted data to an approved internal_app in us; protection meets policy
  DF-5 generated flow (password)                 BLOCK  critical
  • content found (password) raises the label from private to critical
  • critical data may not go to a 'internal_app' destination
  • critical data may only be in us, not region 'eu'
  • credential data at_rest has protection (none); needs hashing: store only a salted, key-stretched hash (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2), never reversible encryption

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Data Protection & DLP Gate
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 3.3 Data types, classifications, states, sovereignty, protection methods · 4.5 DLP · 5.4 Data sovereignty / privacy

briefing.title: Review eight outbound data flows before the new DLP gate goes live
briefing.situation: A retail company is turning on a data loss prevention (DLP) gate that checks data before it leaves a system. Eight flows are queued for review, including card payments, a payroll backup going overseas, a European customer list going to a US analytics tool, and a new service that stores passwords. Some flows are labelled with a lower sensitivity than the data inside them.
your_task: Scan each flow's content for card numbers, Social Security numbers, personal details, passwords, keys and trade secrets, and raise the label if needed.
Check each flow's data state, destination and region against policy, including data sovereignty rules.
Check that the protection fits the data: masking, tokenization, encryption, or hashing for passwords.
Decide ALLOW, ALLOW_WITH_PROTECTION or BLOCK for each flow.
briefing.why_it_matters: Sending card numbers or personal data to the wrong place can bring fines and breach notices. Passwords stored with reversible encryption can all be read at once if the key leaks.
done_when: All 8 flows have an effective label, a decision and a reason.
Flows whose content outranks their label are relabelled.
The password-storage flow (DF-6) is blocked until it uses salted hashing, and the IAM team signs off on the credential-storage design.

glossary.DLP (data loss prevention): Tools and rules that stop sensitive data from leaving where it should stay.
glossary.Data classification: A label for how sensitive data is, such as public, confidential or restricted.
glossary.Data sovereignty: Laws that say certain data must stay in a specific country or region.
glossary.Tokenization: Replacing a real value, like a card number, with a random stand-in.
glossary.Masking: Hiding most of a value on screen, like showing only the last four card digits.
glossary.Hashing: A one-way scramble; with a salt (random extra value) it is the right way to store passwords.

briefing.talking_point: Reviewed 8 outbound data flows: allowed 2, allowed 2 with added protection and blocked 4, including an EU customer list bound for a US tool, a payroll backup headed to an unapproved region and a service storing passwords with reversible encryption.

lessons: Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you have every password (hash + salt instead).
A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking data sovereignty rules.
governance: Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and PII must not reach an external model.
AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.
