--- Step 2 — Reasons, tuning and response -----------------------------------
AL-01 SIEM-006 Threat-intel match → ALERT (high)
  • dns event EV-05: domain=update-checker.example.net is on the threat-intel list
  • RESPONSE: block the IP / sinkhole the domain and quarantine the host via EDR for investigation
AL-02 SIEM-006 Threat-intel match → ALERT (high)
  • firewall event EV-06: dst_ip=192.0.2.66 is on the threat-intel list
  • RESPONSE: block the IP / sinkhole the domain and quarantine the host via EDR for investigation
AL-03 SIEM-004 After-hours privileged action → ALERT (high)
  • privileged action 'add_admin' at Wed 02:14 UTC, outside business hours 07:00-19:00 Mon-Fri
  • RESPONSE: confirm with the account owner and their manager; revert the change if not approved
AL-04 SIEM-001 Brute force → ALERT (critical)
  • 5 events matching {'source': 'auth', 'action': 'login', 'outcome': 'failure'} within 60s (threshold 5 in 300s)
  • followed by a successful login (EV-15) 60s later: possible account compromise
  • RESPONSE: possible compromise: disable the account, revoke sessions, quarantine the user's host via EDR
AL-05 SIEM-002 Password spraying → ALERT (high)
  • 4 distinct user values within 60s (threshold 4 in 600s)
  • RESPONSE: block the source IP and force password resets / MFA enrolment for the targeted users
AL-06 SIEM-007 Port scan → SUPPRESSED (medium)
  • 5 distinct dst_port values within 20s (threshold 5 in 120s)
  • TUNING: SUP-1: authorised vulnerability scanner (weekly credentialed scan) (owner vuln-mgmt team, expires 2026-12-31 00:00:00Z)
AL-07 SIEM-007 Port scan → ALERT (medium)
  • 5 distinct dst_port values within 24s (threshold 5 in 120s)
  • TUNING: SUP-2 (Q3 penetration test engagement) expired 2026-09-30 00:00:00Z: ignored, alert stands
  • RESPONSE: identify the scanning host; block it at the firewall if it is not an authorised scanner
AL-08 SIEM-008 Malware not blocked → ALERT (high)
  • event EV-35 matches {'source': 'edr', 'action': 'malware_detected', 'outcome': 'allowed'}
  • RESPONSE: quarantine the host via EDR, remove the malware, then validate with a rescan before release
AL-09 SIEM-003 Impossible travel → ALERT (high)
  • New York → Frankfurt: 6203 km in 55 min = 6767 km/h (max 900 km/h)
  • TUNING: SUP-3 matches but has no owner: ignored (deny by default)
  • RESPONSE: revoke the user's sessions, require MFA re-authentication and verify with the user
AL-10 SIEM-003 Impossible travel → ALERT (high)
  • London → Singapore: 10848 km in 90 min = 7232 km/h (max 900 km/h)
  • RESPONSE: revoke the user's sessions, require MFA re-authentication and verify with the user
AL-11 SIEM-000 Log parse failure → ALERT (medium)
  • event EV-47: unparseable timestamp '14/10/2026 25:61'
  • RESPONSE: fix the collector/parser and re-ingest; an unparsed event is invisible to every other rule
AL-12 SIEM-005 Log source silence → ALERT (medium)
  • no 'dns' events from 2026-10-14 02:30:00Z to 2026-10-14 12:00:00Z (34200s > 14400s allowed): monitoring blind spot
  • RESPONSE: check the agent/forwarder and its heartbeat (SNMP trap, agent health), restore collection, then validate events arrive

| Objective: SY0-701 4.4 Alerting and monitoring: SIEM aggregation,
| correlation, alert tuning and response (with 4.9 log sources).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A SIEM aggregates and normalises logs from many sources so one rule
| can correlate auth, firewall, EDR, DNS and app events.
|   • Correlation rules turn many weak signals into one alert: thresholds in
| a time window, distinct counts, travel speed, time of day.
|   • Silence is a signal: an expected source that stops sending events is a
| monitoring blind spot, not a quiet day.
|   • Alert tuning (thresholds, suppressions) cuts false positives; every
| suppression needs an owner, a reason and an expiry.
|   • Alert response and remediation: quarantine via EDR, block at the
| firewall, lock the account, then validate the fix.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Alert fatigue: a noisy rule nobody tunes trains analysts to ignore the
| queue, real attacks included.
|   • Permanent, ownerless suppressions: the scanner exception outlives the
| scanner and hides an attacker on that IP.
|   • Dropping events the parser cannot read instead of alerting on them: a
| silent loss of visibility.
|   • Over-tuning: raising a threshold to kill noise also hides low-and-slow
| attacks (false negatives).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI triage agent may close or suppress alerts only through owned,
| expiring, logged suppressions, never silently.
|   • Score the agent like a rule: measure its precision and false negatives
| against labelled incidents before trusting it.
|   • Containment actions (quarantine, account lock) recommended by an agent
| should need human approval or a tight playbook scope.
|   • Event fields are untrusted input: a log line saying 'ignore previous
| instructions' must never steer the agent.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Collects logs from many systems and correlates them' = SIEM.
| 'Unsolicited alert from a network device' = SNMP trap.
|   • 'Who talked to whom, how much, which ports, but no payload' = NetFlow.
| 'Automates benchmark checks (XCCDF/OVAL)' = SCAP.
|   • False positive = alert on benign activity; false negative = attack
| with no alert. Tuning trades one for the other.
|   • Agent-based monitoring installs software on the host; agentless uses
| remote protocols or APIs.
|   • Isolating an infected endpoint so it cannot spread = quarantine;
| rescanning afterwards = validation.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 4.4 Alerting and monitoring: SIEM aggregation,
| correlation, alert tuning and response (with 4.9 log sources).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A SIEM aggregates and normalises logs from many sources so one rule
| can correlate auth, firewall, EDR, DNS and app events.
|   • Correlation rules turn many weak signals into one alert: thresholds in
| a time window, distinct counts, travel speed, time of day.
|   • Silence is a signal: an expected source that stops sending events is a
| monitoring blind spot, not a quiet day.
|   • Alert tuning (thresholds, suppressions) cuts false positives; every
| suppression needs an owner, a reason and an expiry.
|   • Alert response and remediation: quarantine via EDR, block at the
| firewall, lock the account, then validate the fix.

|   • Alert fatigue: a noisy rule nobody tunes trains analysts to ignore the

| scanner and hides an attacker on that IP.

| attacks (false negatives).

|   • An AI triage agent may close or suppress alerts only through owned,
| expiring, logged suppressions, never silently.
|   • Score the agent like a rule: measure its precision and false negatives

|   • Event fields are untrusted input: a log line saying 'ignore previous

| with no alert. Tuning trades one for the other.
|   • Agent-based monitoring installs software on the host; agentless uses
| remote protocols or APIs.
|   • Isolating an infected endpoint so it cannot spread = quarantine;
| rescanning afterwards = validation.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| remote protocols or APIs.
|   • Isolating an infected endpoint so it cannot spread = quarantine;

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.4 Alerting and monitoring: SIEM aggregation,
| correlation, alert tuning and response (with 4.9 log sources).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A SIEM aggregates and normalises logs from many sources so one rule
| can correlate auth, firewall, EDR, DNS and app events.
|   • Correlation rules turn many weak signals into one alert: thresholds in
| a time window, distinct counts, travel speed, time of day.
|   • Silence is a signal: an expected source that stops sending events is a
| monitoring blind spot, not a quiet day.
|   • Alert tuning (thresholds, suppressions) cuts false positives; every
| suppression needs an owner, a reason and an expiry.
|   • Alert response and remediation: quarantine via EDR, block at the
| firewall, lock the account, then validate the fix.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Alert fatigue: a noisy rule nobody tunes trains analysts to ignore the
| queue, real attacks included.
|   • Permanent, ownerless suppressions: the scanner exception outlives the
| scanner and hides an attacker on that IP.
|   • Dropping events the parser cannot read instead of alerting on them: a
| silent loss of visibility.
|   • Over-tuning: raising a threshold to kill noise also hides low-and-slow
| attacks (false negatives).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI triage agent may close or suppress alerts only through owned,
| expiring, logged suppressions, never silently.
|   • Score the agent like a rule: measure its precision and false negatives
| against labelled incidents before trusting it.
|   • Containment actions (quarantine, account lock) recommended by an agent
| should need human approval or a tight playbook scope.
|   • Event fields are untrusted input: a log line saying 'ignore previous
| instructions' must never steer the agent.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Collects logs from many systems and correlates them' = SIEM.
| 'Unsolicited alert from a network device' = SNMP trap.
|   • 'Who talked to whom, how much, which ports, but no payload' = NetFlow.
| 'Automates benchmark checks (XCCDF/OVAL)' = SCAP.
|   • False positive = alert on benign activity; false negative = attack
| with no alert. Tuning trades one for the other.
|   • Agent-based monitoring installs software on the host; agentless uses
| remote protocols or APIs.
|   • Isolating an infected endpoint so it cannot spread = quarantine;
| rescanning afterwards = validation.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

AL-02  SIEM-004 After-hours privileged action  high      03:30:00Z  user=frank, host=ERP-1                    EV-30                    ALERT
AL-03  SIEM-002 Password spraying              high      04:01:00Z  src_ip=198.51.100.23                      EV-24, EV-25, EV-26 ...  ALERT
AL-04  SIEM-007 Port scan                      medium    07:00:20Z  src_ip=10.0.5.20                          EV-31, EV-32, EV-33 ...  SUPPRESSED
AL-05  SIEM-006 Threat-intel match             high      08:00:00Z  indicator=203.0.113.200, source_host=10.  EV-40                    ALERT
AL-06  SIEM-000 Log parse failure              medium    16:00:00Z  host=HR-APP-2                             EV-42                    ALERT

--- Step 2 — Reasons, tuning and response -----------------------------------
AL-01 SIEM-001 Brute force → ALERT (critical)
  • 5 events matching {'source': 'auth', 'action': 'login', 'outcome': 'failure'} within 60s (threshold 5 in 300s)
  • followed by a successful login (EV-23) 45s later: possible account compromise
  • RESPONSE: possible compromise: disable the account, revoke sessions, quarantine the user's host via EDR
AL-02 SIEM-004 After-hours privileged action → ALERT (high)
  • privileged action 'disable_logging' at Wed 03:30 UTC, outside business hours 07:00-19:00 Mon-Fri
  • RESPONSE: confirm with the account owner and their manager; revert the change if not approved
AL-03 SIEM-002 Password spraying → ALERT (high)
  • 4 distinct user values within 60s (threshold 4 in 600s)
  • RESPONSE: block the source IP and force password resets / MFA enrolment for the targeted users
AL-04 SIEM-007 Port scan → SUPPRESSED (medium)
  • 5 distinct dst_port values within 20s (threshold 5 in 120s)
  • TUNING: SUP-1: authorised vulnerability scanner (weekly credentialed scan) (owner vuln-mgmt team, expires 2026-12-31 00:00:00Z)
AL-05 SIEM-006 Threat-intel match → ALERT (high)
  • firewall event EV-40: dst_ip=203.0.113.200 is on the threat-intel list
  • RESPONSE: block the IP / sinkhole the domain and quarantine the host via EDR for investigation
AL-06 SIEM-000 Log parse failure → ALERT (medium)
  • event EV-42: unparseable timestamp '14/10/2026 10:15'
  • RESPONSE: fix the collector/parser and re-ingest; an unparsed event is invisible to every other rule
AL-07 SIEM-005 Log source silence → ALERT (medium)
  • no 'auth' events from 2026-10-14 06:00:00Z to 2026-10-14 16:00:00Z (36000s > 21600s allowed): monitoring blind spot
  • RESPONSE: check the agent/forwarder and its heartbeat (SNMP trap, agent health), restore collection, then validate events arrive

--- Step 3 — Alert quality against ground truth -----------------------------

Before vs after tuning
Stage  TP  FP  FN  Precision  Recall
-----  --  --  --  ---------  ------
raw    5   2   2   71.4%      71.4%
tuned  5   1   2   83.3%      71.4%
  • AL-04 suppressed: scenario S6 is benign, so FP 2 → 1 and precision 71.4% → 83.3%
  • FALSE NEGATIVE S1: the auth log forwarder stops sending events (no rule fired)
  • FALSE NEGATIVE S7: port scan from 10.0.5.99 (Q3 penetration test engagement) (no rule fired)

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.4 Alerting and monitoring: SIEM aggregation,
| correlation, alert tuning and response (with 4.9 log sources).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A SIEM aggregates and normalises logs from many sources so one rule
| can correlate auth, firewall, EDR, DNS and app events.
|   • Correlation rules turn many weak signals into one alert: thresholds in
| a time window, distinct counts, travel speed, time of day.
|   • Silence is a signal: an expected source that stops sending events is a
| monitoring blind spot, not a quiet day.
|   • Alert tuning (thresholds, suppressions) cuts false positives; every
| suppression needs an owner, a reason and an expiry.
|   • Alert response and remediation: quarantine via EDR, block at the
| firewall, lock the account, then validate the fix.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Alert fatigue: a noisy rule nobody tunes trains analysts to ignore the
| queue, real attacks included.
|   • Permanent, ownerless suppressions: the scanner exception outlives the
| scanner and hides an attacker on that IP.
|   • Dropping events the parser cannot read instead of alerting on them: a
| silent loss of visibility.
|   • Over-tuning: raising a threshold to kill noise also hides low-and-slow
| attacks (false negatives).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI triage agent may close or suppress alerts only through owned,
| expiring, logged suppressions, never silently.
|   • Score the agent like a rule: measure its precision and false negatives
| against labelled incidents before trusting it.
|   • Containment actions (quarantine, account lock) recommended by an agent
| should need human approval or a tight playbook scope.
|   • Event fields are untrusted input: a log line saying 'ignore previous
| instructions' must never steer the agent.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Collects logs from many systems and correlates them' = SIEM.
| 'Unsolicited alert from a network device' = SNMP trap.
|   • 'Who talked to whom, how much, which ports, but no payload' = NetFlow.
| 'Automates benchmark checks (XCCDF/OVAL)' = SCAP.
|   • False positive = alert on benign activity; false negative = attack
| with no alert. Tuning trades one for the other.
|   • Agent-based monitoring installs software on the host; agentless uses
| remote protocols or APIs.
|   • Isolating an infected endpoint so it cannot spread = quarantine;
| rescanning afterwards = validation.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: SIEM Correlation & Alert Tuning
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.4 Alerting and monitoring: SIEM, correlation, alert tuning, response · 4.9 Log data sources

briefing.title: Overnight SIEM alerts: brute force, password spraying and impossible travel
briefing.situation: Our security monitoring system collected 52 log events overnight from sign-in, firewall, DNS (domain name system), endpoint and application sources. Several point to attacks on user accounts: repeated failed logins followed by a success, one address trying many accounts, and users signing in from two continents within an hour. We also suspect noisy alerts and a gap where one log source went quiet.
your_task: Correlate the 52 events into alerts using the detection rules.
Apply the suppression list, but only entries that have an owner and have not expired.
Write the response for each alert, such as disable the account, revoke sessions or quarantine the host.
Measure alert quality before and after tuning, and name any attack that no rule caught.
briefing.why_it_matters: A successful login right after a burst of failures may mean an attacker is already inside an account. Too many false alarms bury the real ones, and a silent log source is a blind spot.
done_when: All 12 alerts have a disposition, a reason and a response.
Only the owned, unexpired scanner suppression is applied; the expired and ownerless ones are ignored.

Account alerts (brute force on jdoe, spraying, impossible travel for bnguyen and asmith, after-hours admin grant by mlee) are handed to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) team for account disable, session revocation, multi-factor authentication (MFA) checks and access review.
The missed low-and-slow password guessing against pchan is logged as a detection gap.

glossary.SIEM: Security information and event management: a system that gathers logs and raises alerts.
glossary.Correlation rule: Logic that links related events, such as five failed logins in five minutes.
glossary.Brute force: Trying many passwords against one account.
glossary.Password spraying: Trying one or two common passwords against many accounts.
glossary.Impossible travel: Sign-ins from places too far apart to reach in the time between them.
glossary.Suppression: A rule that silences a known, harmless alert; it should have an owner and an end date.
glossary.Precision / recall: Precision is the share of alerts that were real; recall is the share of real attacks that raised an alert.

briefing.talking_point: Correlated 52 log events into 12 alerts, suppressed 1 authorized-scanner false positive to raise precision from 83.3% to 90.9%, sent the brute-force, spraying and impossible-travel account alerts to IAM for session revocation and MFA checks, and flagged a missed low-and-slow password attack as a detection gap.

lessons: Alert fatigue: a noisy rule nobody tunes trains analysts to ignore the queue, real attacks included.
Permanent, ownerless suppressions: the scanner exception outlives the scanner and hides an attacker on that IP.
Dropping events the parser cannot read instead of alerting on them: a silent loss of visibility.
governance: An AI triage agent may close or suppress alerts only through owned, expiring, logged suppressions, never silently.
Score the agent like a rule: measure its precision and false negatives against labelled incidents before trusting it.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

----------------------------------  --------------  --------------  ----

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.1 Security implications of architecture models:
| cloud, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Responsibility matrix: the provider always owns the physical layer;
| the customer always owns its data and user access.
|   • IaaS = you patch the guest OS; PaaS = you secure your code; SaaS = you
| configure users and data. Serverless = no OS for you to patch.
|   • Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and scannable: fix
| the template once and every copy is fixed.
|   • Network infrastructure: air-gapped (physical isolation), logical
| segmentation (VLANs/subnets), SDN (central software control plane).
|   • High availability spreads critical resources across zones;
| considerations trade availability and resilience against cost.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A public storage bucket or public database: the most common cloud data
| exposure.
|   • Security groups allowing SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it was
| quicker to test'.
|   • IAM policies with action '*' on resource '*' handed to CI pipelines:
| one leaked token = full account takeover.
|   • Privileged or root containers sharing the host kernel, and plaintext
| secrets in function environment variables.
|   • New resource types deployed without anyone reviewing them (unreviewed
| = unprotected).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that writes IaC must pass the same policy-as-code gate as
| a human: the gate, not the agent, decides.
|   • Give infrastructure agents scoped roles, never '*' on '*'; their blast
| radius is the permissions you grant.
|   • Deny by default: a resource or property the agent invents that the
| policy does not know is blocked, not trusted.
|   • Every finding carries its fix, so an agent can propose a remediation
| that a human reviews before re-running the gate.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Who patches the guest OS on IaaS?' = the customer. 'Who secures the
| physical data centre?' = always the provider.
|   • ICS/SCADA, IoT and embedded systems often cannot be patched:
| compensate with segmentation and monitoring.
|   • Air-gapped = physical isolation; VLAN/subnet = logical segmentation;
| SDN = control plane separated from data plane.
|   • Containers share the host kernel (lighter, less isolation); VMs have
| their own OS on a hypervisor (VM escape, sprawl).
|   • Microservices: smaller blast radius, larger API attack surface. RTOS:
| deterministic timing for real-time control.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 3.1 Security implications of architecture models:
| cloud, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA.

|   • Responsibility matrix: the provider always owns the physical layer;

|   • IaaS = you patch the guest OS; PaaS = you secure your code; SaaS = you

|   • Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and scannable: fix
| the template once and every copy is fixed.
|   • Network infrastructure: air-gapped (physical isolation), logical
| segmentation (VLANs/subnets), SDN (central software control plane).

| considerations trade availability and resilience against cost.

| that a human reviews before re-running the gate.

| their own OS on a hypervisor (VM escape, sprawl).
|   • Microservices: smaller blast radius, larger API attack surface. RTOS:
| deterministic timing for real-time control.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.1 Security implications of architecture models:
| cloud, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Responsibility matrix: the provider always owns the physical layer;
| the customer always owns its data and user access.
|   • IaaS = you patch the guest OS; PaaS = you secure your code; SaaS = you
| configure users and data. Serverless = no OS for you to patch.
|   • Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and scannable: fix
| the template once and every copy is fixed.
|   • Network infrastructure: air-gapped (physical isolation), logical
| segmentation (VLANs/subnets), SDN (central software control plane).
|   • High availability spreads critical resources across zones;
| considerations trade availability and resilience against cost.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A public storage bucket or public database: the most common cloud data
| exposure.
|   • Security groups allowing SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it was
| quicker to test'.
|   • IAM policies with action '*' on resource '*' handed to CI pipelines:
| one leaked token = full account takeover.
|   • Privileged or root containers sharing the host kernel, and plaintext
| secrets in function environment variables.
|   • New resource types deployed without anyone reviewing them (unreviewed
| = unprotected).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that writes IaC must pass the same policy-as-code gate as
| a human: the gate, not the agent, decides.
|   • Give infrastructure agents scoped roles, never '*' on '*'; their blast
| radius is the permissions you grant.
|   • Deny by default: a resource or property the agent invents that the
| policy does not know is blocked, not trusted.
|   • Every finding carries its fix, so an agent can propose a remediation
| that a human reviews before re-running the gate.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Who patches the guest OS on IaaS?' = the customer. 'Who secures the
| physical data centre?' = always the provider.
|   • ICS/SCADA, IoT and embedded systems often cannot be patched:
| compensate with segmentation and monitoring.
|   • Air-gapped = physical isolation; VLAN/subnet = logical segmentation;
| SDN = control plane separated from data plane.
|   • Containers share the host kernel (lighter, less isolation); VMs have
| their own OS on a hypervisor (VM escape, sprawl).
|   • Microservices: smaller blast radius, larger API attack surface. RTOS:
| deterministic timing for real-time control.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.1 Security implications of architecture models:
| cloud, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Responsibility matrix: the provider always owns the physical layer;
| the customer always owns its data and user access.
|   • IaaS = you patch the guest OS; PaaS = you secure your code; SaaS = you
| configure users and data. Serverless = no OS for you to patch.
|   • Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and scannable: fix
| the template once and every copy is fixed.
|   • Network infrastructure: air-gapped (physical isolation), logical
| segmentation (VLANs/subnets), SDN (central software control plane).
|   • High availability spreads critical resources across zones;
| considerations trade availability and resilience against cost.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A public storage bucket or public database: the most common cloud data
| exposure.
|   • Security groups allowing SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it was
| quicker to test'.
|   • IAM policies with action '*' on resource '*' handed to CI pipelines:
| one leaked token = full account takeover.
|   • Privileged or root containers sharing the host kernel, and plaintext
| secrets in function environment variables.
|   • New resource types deployed without anyone reviewing them (unreviewed
| = unprotected).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that writes IaC must pass the same policy-as-code gate as
| a human: the gate, not the agent, decides.
|   • Give infrastructure agents scoped roles, never '*' on '*'; their blast
| radius is the permissions you grant.
|   • Deny by default: a resource or property the agent invents that the
| policy does not know is blocked, not trusted.
|   • Every finding carries its fix, so an agent can propose a remediation
| that a human reviews before re-running the gate.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Who patches the guest OS on IaaS?' = the customer. 'Who secures the
| physical data centre?' = always the provider.
|   • ICS/SCADA, IoT and embedded systems often cannot be patched:
| compensate with segmentation and monitoring.
|   • Air-gapped = physical isolation; VLAN/subnet = logical segmentation;
| SDN = control plane separated from data plane.
|   • Containers share the host kernel (lighter, less isolation); VMs have
| their own OS on a hypervisor (VM escape, sprawl).
|   • Microservices: smaller blast radius, larger API attack surface. RTOS:
| deterministic timing for real-time control.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.1 Security implications of architecture models:
| cloud, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Responsibility matrix: the provider always owns the physical layer;
| the customer always owns its data and user access.
|   • IaaS = you patch the guest OS; PaaS = you secure your code; SaaS = you
| configure users and data. Serverless = no OS for you to patch.
|   • Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and scannable: fix
| the template once and every copy is fixed.
|   • Network infrastructure: air-gapped (physical isolation), logical
| segmentation (VLANs/subnets), SDN (central software control plane).
|   • High availability spreads critical resources across zones;
| considerations trade availability and resilience against cost.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A public storage bucket or public database: the most common cloud data
| exposure.
|   • Security groups allowing SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it was
| quicker to test'.
|   • IAM policies with action '*' on resource '*' handed to CI pipelines:
| one leaked token = full account takeover.
|   • Privileged or root containers sharing the host kernel, and plaintext
| secrets in function environment variables.
|   • New resource types deployed without anyone reviewing them (unreviewed
| = unprotected).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that writes IaC must pass the same policy-as-code gate as
| a human: the gate, not the agent, decides.
|   • Give infrastructure agents scoped roles, never '*' on '*'; their blast
| radius is the permissions you grant.
|   • Deny by default: a resource or property the agent invents that the
| policy does not know is blocked, not trusted.
|   • Every finding carries its fix, so an agent can propose a remediation
| that a human reviews before re-running the gate.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Who patches the guest OS on IaaS?' = the customer. 'Who secures the
| physical data centre?' = always the provider.
|   • ICS/SCADA, IoT and embedded systems often cannot be patched:
| compensate with segmentation and monitoring.
|   • Air-gapped = physical isolation; VLAN/subnet = logical segmentation;
| SDN = control plane separated from data plane.
|   • Containers share the host kernel (lighter, less isolation); VMs have
| their own OS on a hypervisor (VM escape, sprawl).
|   • Microservices: smaller blast radius, larger API attack surface. RTOS:
| deterministic timing for real-time control.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Responsibility
Layer                               IaaS            PaaS            SaaS
----------------------------------  --------------  --------------  ----
Physical data centre and hardware   cloud provider  cloud provider  cloud provider
Virtualisation layer / hypervisor   cloud provider  cloud provider  cloud provider
Network controls (security groups)  customer        shared          cloud provider
Guest operating system patching     customer        cloud provider  cloud provider
Runtime and middleware              customer        cloud provider  cloud provider
Application code                    customer        customer        cloud provider
Data classification and protection  customer        customer        customer
User identities and access          customer        customer        customer

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.1 Security implications of architecture models:
| cloud, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Responsibility matrix: the provider always owns the physical layer;
| the customer always owns its data and user access.
|   • IaaS = you patch the guest OS; PaaS = you secure your code; SaaS = you
| configure users and data. Serverless = no OS for you to patch.
|   • Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and scannable: fix
| the template once and every copy is fixed.
|   • Network infrastructure: air-gapped (physical isolation), logical
| segmentation (VLANs/subnets), SDN (central software control plane).
|   • High availability spreads critical resources across zones;
| considerations trade availability and resilience against cost.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A public storage bucket or public database: the most common cloud data
| exposure.
|   • Security groups allowing SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it was
| quicker to test'.
|   • IAM policies with action '*' on resource '*' handed to CI pipelines:
| one leaked token = full account takeover.
|   • Privileged or root containers sharing the host kernel, and plaintext
| secrets in function environment variables.
|   • New resource types deployed without anyone reviewing them (unreviewed
| = unprotected).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that writes IaC must pass the same policy-as-code gate as
| a human: the gate, not the agent, decides.
|   • Give infrastructure agents scoped roles, never '*' on '*'; their blast
| radius is the permissions you grant.
|   • Deny by default: a resource or property the agent invents that the
| policy does not know is blocked, not trusted.
|   • Every finding carries its fix, so an agent can propose a remediation
| that a human reviews before re-running the gate.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Who patches the guest OS on IaaS?' = the customer. 'Who secures the
| physical data centre?' = always the provider.
|   • ICS/SCADA, IoT and embedded systems often cannot be patched:
| compensate with segmentation and monitoring.
|   • Air-gapped = physical isolation; VLAN/subnet = logical segmentation;
| SDN = control plane separated from data plane.
|   • Containers share the host kernel (lighter, less isolation); VMs have
| their own OS on a hypervisor (VM escape, sprawl).
|   • Microservices: smaller blast radius, larger API attack surface. RTOS:
| deterministic timing for real-time control.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

vm-3         vm              PASS    none (PASS)  -
iam-4        iam_policy      PASS    none (PASS)  -
security-5   security_group  PASS    none (PASS)  -

--- Step 2 — Findings and fixes ---------------------------------------------
vm-1 (vm) → FAIL
  • MEDIUM IAC-V2 VM has a public IP: public_ip = true
  • Fix: Set public_ip = false and reach the VM through the load balancer or a bastion.
  • MEDIUM IAC-T1 Missing required tags: missing tag(s): owner
  • Fix: Add tags owner and data_classification.
container-2 (container) → FAIL
  • HIGH IAC-C1 Privileged container: 'privileged' not declared: cannot verify (deny by default)
  • Fix: Set privileged = false and add only the specific capabilities needed.
vm-7 (vm) → FAIL
  • MEDIUM IAC-T1 Missing required tags: missing tag(s): owner
  • Fix: Add tags owner and data_classification.

--- Step 3 — Deployment decision --------------------------------------------
  Gate                                           WARN  1 high finding(s); 3 medium finding(s); deploy only with a tracked remediation

--- Step 4 — Shared-responsibility matrix (who secures what) ----------------

Responsibility
Layer                               IaaS            PaaS            SaaS
----------------------------------  --------------  --------------  ----
Physical data centre and hardware   cloud provider  cloud provider  cloud provider
Virtualisation layer / hypervisor   cloud provider  cloud provider  cloud provider
Network controls (security groups)  customer        shared          cloud provider
Guest operating system patching     customer        cloud provider  cloud provider
Runtime and middleware              customer        cloud provider  cloud provider
Application code                    customer        customer        cloud provider
Data classification and protection  customer        customer        customer
User identities and access          customer        customer        customer

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.1 Security implications of architecture models:
| cloud, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Responsibility matrix: the provider always owns the physical layer;
| the customer always owns its data and user access.
|   • IaaS = you patch the guest OS; PaaS = you secure your code; SaaS = you
| configure users and data. Serverless = no OS for you to patch.
|   • Infrastructure as code makes deployments repeatable and scannable: fix
| the template once and every copy is fixed.
|   • Network infrastructure: air-gapped (physical isolation), logical
| segmentation (VLANs/subnets), SDN (central software control plane).
|   • High availability spreads critical resources across zones;
| considerations trade availability and resilience against cost.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • A public storage bucket or public database: the most common cloud data
| exposure.
|   • Security groups allowing SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it was
| quicker to test'.
|   • IAM policies with action '*' on resource '*' handed to CI pipelines:
| one leaked token = full account takeover.
|   • Privileged or root containers sharing the host kernel, and plaintext
| secrets in function environment variables.
|   • New resource types deployed without anyone reviewing them (unreviewed
| = unprotected).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that writes IaC must pass the same policy-as-code gate as
| a human: the gate, not the agent, decides.
|   • Give infrastructure agents scoped roles, never '*' on '*'; their blast
| radius is the permissions you grant.
|   • Deny by default: a resource or property the agent invents that the
| policy does not know is blocked, not trusted.
|   • Every finding carries its fix, so an agent can propose a remediation
| that a human reviews before re-running the gate.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Who patches the guest OS on IaaS?' = the customer. 'Who secures the
| physical data centre?' = always the provider.
|   • ICS/SCADA, IoT and embedded systems often cannot be patched:
| compensate with segmentation and monitoring.
|   • Air-gapped = physical isolation; VLAN/subnet = logical segmentation;
| SDN = control plane separated from data plane.
|   • Containers share the host kernel (lighter, less isolation); VMs have
| their own OS on a hypervisor (VM escape, sprawl).
|   • Microservices: smaller blast radius, larger API attack surface. RTOS:
| deterministic timing for real-time control.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Cloud Architecture & IaC Misconfiguration Gate
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 3.1 Architecture models: cloud responsibility matrix, IaC, serverless, containers, segmentation, HA · 3.3 Data at rest/in transit · 4.1 Secure baselines · 4.6 Least privilege

briefing.title: Gate the 'northwind-shop-prod' cloud deployment before it ships
briefing.situation: The cloud team wants to deploy the production online shop from an infrastructure-as-code plan with 11 resources. Before it goes live, every resource must pass the security checks: no admin ports open to the internet, no public storage or databases, encryption on, and no over-powered permissions. One permission policy for the build pipeline grants full access to everything.
your_task: Scan all 11 resources in the plan against the security checks.
Record each failed check with its severity and the fix.
Deny any resource type that has no reviewed checks.
Make the deploy decision using the gate rules: any critical finding, or more high findings than allowed, blocks the release.
briefing.why_it_matters: One open admin port or public database can be found by attackers within hours. A build-pipeline account with full access means anyone who steals that pipeline can control the whole cloud account.
done_when: All 11 resources show PASS or FAIL with the checks that failed.
The gate decision is BLOCK, with the 5 critical and 3 high findings listed.
The wildcard IAM policy (iam-ci-deployer) is sent to the IAM team to be rewritten with only the actions and resources the deployer needs.

glossary.IaC (infrastructure as code): Defining servers, networks and permissions in files, so they can be reviewed before they are built.
glossary.Security group: A cloud firewall that controls which traffic can reach a resource.
glossary.IAM policy: A rule in Identity and Access Management that says which actions an account may take on which resources.
glossary.Least privilege: Giving an account only the access it needs, nothing more.
glossary.Availability zone: A separate data centre within a cloud region; using two keeps a service up if one fails.
glossary.Shared responsibility model: The split of security duties between the cloud provider and the customer.

briefing.talking_point: Scanned an 11-resource infrastructure-as-code plan, passed 3 resources and failed 8, and blocked the release on 5 critical and 3 high findings, including a build-pipeline (CI, continuous integration) deployer IAM policy that allowed every action on every resource.

lessons: A public storage bucket or public database: the most common cloud data exposure.
Security groups allowing SSH/RDP from 0.0.0.0/0 because 'it was quicker to test'.
IAM policies with action '*' on resource '*' handed to CI pipelines: one leaked token = full account takeover.
governance: An AI agent that writes IaC must pass the same policy-as-code gate as a human: the gate, not the agent, decides.
Give infrastructure agents scoped roles, never '*' on '*'; their blast radius is the permissions you grant.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement,
| assignment/accounting, tracking and disposal.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Procurement is the first control: buy through an approved process so
| every asset enters the inventory with an owner.
|   • Assignment/accounting gives every asset an accountable owner and a
| data classification.
|   • Monitoring/tracking compares the inventory with enumeration (discovery
| scans) to find unmanaged and missing assets.
|   • NIST SP 800-88 levels: Clear (logical overwrite) < Purge (crypto-
| erase, secure erase, degauss) < Destroy (shred, pulverize, incinerate).
|   • Disposal needs certification (certificate of destruction) and must
| respect data retention and legal holds.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
|   • Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data
| survives.
|   • Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use
| crypto-erase or destroy.
|   • Paying a shredding vendor without getting a certificate of
| destruction: no proof, no accountability.
|   • Destroying records still under retention or legal hold (spoliation of
| evidence).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner
| and a classification.
|   • An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT:
| onboard it or block it.
|   • When decommissioning an AI system, sanitize its training data, vector
| stores, logs and backups too.
|   • An AI asset agent may reconcile and recommend, but disposal approval
| stays with a human owner.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Device on the network not in the inventory' = unmanaged asset /
| shadow IT; NAC can quarantine it.
|   • 'SSD leaving the organisation' = crypto-erase/secure erase (purge) or
| physical destruction, never degauss.
|   • Certificate of destruction = documented proof that media was
| destroyed, usually from a third party.
|   • Legal hold overrides the retention schedule: nothing under hold may be
| deleted or destroyed.
|   • Clear protects against simple recovery tools; Purge against laboratory
| recovery; Destroy makes reuse impossible.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement,
| assignment/accounting, tracking and disposal.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Procurement is the first control: buy through an approved process so
| every asset enters the inventory with an owner.
|   • Assignment/accounting gives every asset an accountable owner and a
| data classification.
|   • Monitoring/tracking compares the inventory with enumeration (discovery
| scans) to find unmanaged and missing assets.
|   • NIST SP 800-88 levels: Clear (logical overwrite) < Purge (crypto-
| erase, secure erase, degauss) < Destroy (shred, pulverize, incinerate).
|   • Disposal needs certification (certificate of destruction) and must
| respect data retention and legal holds.
|

|   • Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
|   • Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data
| survives.
|   • Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use
| crypto-erase or destroy.
|   • Paying a shredding vendor without getting a certificate of
| destruction: no proof, no accountability.
|   • Destroying records still under retention or legal hold (spoliation of
| evidence).

| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner
| and a classification.
|   • An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT:
| onboard it or block it.
|   • When decommissioning an AI system, sanitize its training data, vector
| stores, logs and backups too.
|   • An AI asset agent may reconcile and recommend, but disposal approval
| stays with a human owner.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Device on the network not in the inventory' = unmanaged asset /
| shadow IT; NAC can quarantine it.
|   • 'SSD leaving the organisation' = crypto-erase/secure erase (purge) or
| physical destruction, never degauss.
|   • Certificate of destruction = documented proof that media was
| destroyed, usually from a third party.
|   • Legal hold overrides the retention schedule: nothing under hold may be
| deleted or destroyed.
|   • Clear protects against simple recovery tools; Purge against laboratory
| recovery; Destroy makes reuse impossible.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement,
| assignment/accounting, tracking and disposal.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Procurement is the first control: buy through an approved process so
| every asset enters the inventory with an owner.
|   • Assignment/accounting gives every asset an accountable owner and a
| data classification.
|   • Monitoring/tracking compares the inventory with enumeration (discovery
| scans) to find unmanaged and missing assets.
|   • NIST SP 800-88 levels: Clear (logical overwrite) < Purge (crypto-
| erase, secure erase, degauss) < Destroy (shred, pulverize, incinerate).
|   • Disposal needs certification (certificate of destruction) and must
| respect data retention and legal holds.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
|   • Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data
| survives.
|   • Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use
| crypto-erase or destroy.
|   • Paying a shredding vendor without getting a certificate of
| destruction: no proof, no accountability.
|   • Destroying records still under retention or legal hold (spoliation of
| evidence).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner
| and a classification.
|   • An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT:
| onboard it or block it.
|   • When decommissioning an AI system, sanitize its training data, vector
| stores, logs and backups too.
|   • An AI asset agent may reconcile and recommend, but disposal approval
| stays with a human owner.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Device on the network not in the inventory' = unmanaged asset /
| shadow IT; NAC can quarantine it.
|   • 'SSD leaving the organisation' = crypto-erase/secure erase (purge) or
| physical destruction, never degauss.
|   • Certificate of destruction = documented proof that media was
| destroyed, usually from a third party.
|   • Legal hold overrides the retention schedule: nothing under hold may be
| deleted or destroyed.
|   • Clear protects against simple recovery tools; Purge against laboratory
| recovery; Destroy makes reuse impossible.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement,
| assignment/accounting, tracking and disposal.

| Key Concepts
|   • Procurement is the first control: buy through an approved process so

|   • Assignment/accounting gives every asset an accountable owner and a
| data classification.

|   • NIST SP 800-88 levels: Clear (logical overwrite) < Purge (crypto-

| respect data retention and legal holds.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
|   • Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data
| survives.
|   • Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use
| crypto-erase or destroy.
|   • Paying a shredding vendor without getting a certificate of
| destruction: no proof, no accountability.
|   • Destroying records still under retention or legal hold (spoliation of
| evidence).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner
| and a classification.
|   • An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT:
| onboard it or block it.
|   • When decommissioning an AI system, sanitize its training data, vector
| stores, logs and backups too.
|   • An AI asset agent may reconcile and recommend, but disposal approval
| stays with a human owner.
|

| destroyed, usually from a third party.

| deleted or destroyed.
|   • Clear protects against simple recovery tools; Purge against laboratory
| recovery; Destroy makes reuse impossible.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement,
| assignment/accounting, tracking and disposal.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Procurement is the first control: buy through an approved process so
| every asset enters the inventory with an owner.
|   • Assignment/accounting gives every asset an accountable owner and a
| data classification.
|   • Monitoring/tracking compares the inventory with enumeration (discovery
| scans) to find unmanaged and missing assets.
|   • NIST SP 800-88 levels: Clear (logical overwrite) < Purge (crypto-
| erase, secure erase, degauss) < Destroy (shred, pulverize, incinerate).
|   • Disposal needs certification (certificate of destruction) and must
| respect data retention and legal holds.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
|   • Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data
| survives.
|   • Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use
| crypto-erase or destroy.
|   • Paying a shredding vendor without getting a certificate of
| destruction: no proof, no accountability.
|   • Destroying records still under retention or legal hold (spoliation of
| evidence).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner
| and a classification.
|   • An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT:
| onboard it or block it.
|   • When decommissioning an AI system, sanitize its training data, vector
| stores, logs and backups too.
|   • An AI asset agent may reconcile and recommend, but disposal approval
| stays with a human owner.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Device on the network not in the inventory' = unmanaged asset /
| shadow IT; NAC can quarantine it.
|   • 'SSD leaving the organisation' = crypto-erase/secure erase (purge) or
| physical destruction, never degauss.
|   • Certificate of destruction = documented proof that media was
| destroyed, usually from a third party.
|   • Legal hold overrides the retention schedule: nothing under hold may be
| deleted or destroyed.
|   • Clear protects against simple recovery tools; Purge against laboratory
| recovery; Destroy makes reuse impossible.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement,
| assignment/accounting, tracking and disposal.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Procurement is the first control: buy through an approved process so
| every asset enters the inventory with an owner.
|   • Assignment/accounting gives every asset an accountable owner and a
| data classification.
|   • Monitoring/tracking compares the inventory with enumeration (discovery
| scans) to find unmanaged and missing assets.
|   • NIST SP 800-88 levels: Clear (logical overwrite) < Purge (crypto-
| erase, secure erase, degauss) < Destroy (shred, pulverize, incinerate).
|   • Disposal needs certification (certificate of destruction) and must
| respect data retention and legal holds.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
|   • Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data
| survives.
|   • Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use
| crypto-erase or destroy.
|   • Paying a shredding vendor without getting a certificate of
| destruction: no proof, no accountability.
|   • Destroying records still under retention or legal hold (spoliation of
| evidence).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner
| and a classification.
|   • An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT:
| onboard it or block it.
|   • When decommissioning an AI system, sanitize its training data, vector
| stores, logs and backups too.
|   • An AI asset agent may reconcile and recommend, but disposal approval
| stays with a human owner.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Device on the network not in the inventory' = unmanaged asset /
| shadow IT; NAC can quarantine it.
|   • 'SSD leaving the organisation' = crypto-erase/secure erase (purge) or
| physical destruction, never degauss.
|   • Certificate of destruction = documented proof that media was
| destroyed, usually from a third party.
|   • Legal hold overrides the retention schedule: nothing under hold may be
| deleted or destroyed.
|   • Clear protects against simple recovery tools; Purge against laboratory
| recovery; Destroy makes reuse impossible.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement,
| assignment/accounting, tracking and disposal.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Procurement is the first control: buy through an approved process so
| every asset enters the inventory with an owner.
|   • Assignment/accounting gives every asset an accountable owner and a
| data classification.
|   • Monitoring/tracking compares the inventory with enumeration (discovery
| scans) to find unmanaged and missing assets.
|   • NIST SP 800-88 levels: Clear (logical overwrite) < Purge (crypto-
| erase, secure erase, degauss) < Destroy (shred, pulverize, incinerate).
|   • Disposal needs certification (certificate of destruction) and must
| respect data retention and legal holds.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
|   • Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data
| survives.
|   • Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use
| crypto-erase or destroy.
|   • Paying a shredding vendor without getting a certificate of
| destruction: no proof, no accountability.
|   • Destroying records still under retention or legal hold (spoliation of
| evidence).
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner
| and a classification.
|   • An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT:
| onboard it or block it.
|   • When decommissioning an AI system, sanitize its training data, vector
| stores, logs and backups too.
|   • An AI asset agent may reconcile and recommend, but disposal approval
| stays with a human owner.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Device on the network not in the inventory' = unmanaged asset /
| shadow IT; NAC can quarantine it.
|   • 'SSD leaving the organisation' = crypto-erase/secure erase (purge) or
| physical destruction, never degauss.
|   • Certificate of destruction = documented proof that media was
| destroyed, usually from a third party.
|   • Legal hold overrides the retention schedule: nothing under hold may be
| deleted or destroyed.
|   • Clear protects against simple recovery tools; Purge against laboratory
| recovery; Destroy makes reuse impossible.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Asset Inventory & Secure Disposal
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.2 Asset management: procurement, ownership, classification, inventory, enumeration, sanitization, destruction, certification, retention · 3.3 Data classification · 4.5 NAC

briefing.title: Reconcile the asset inventory with the network scan and approve disposal requests
briefing.situation: Our asset records (the CMDB) list 8 devices, but a network scan found extra devices nobody registered, and one laptop has not been seen in 20 days. Some assets have no owner or no data label. Separately, nine requests to wipe or destroy old drives, tapes, USB sticks and paper are waiting for approval.
your_task: Compare the CMDB with the scan and flag missing, unowned, unclassified and unmanaged devices.
Give each finding an action, such as locate the asset, assign an owner, or quarantine with network access control.
Check each disposal request: the method must meet the needed level (clear, purge, destroy) for the media type and data label.
Reject any request under legal hold, still inside its retention period, or missing a certificate of destruction.
briefing.why_it_matters: A lost laptop or an unknown device on the network can leak data or give attackers a foothold. A drive wiped the wrong way can be recovered by whoever buys it.
done_when: Every CMDB entry and scanned device has a finding and an action.
All 9 disposal requests have a decision and a reason.
The IAM team is asked to revoke sessions and device access for the owner of missing laptop-17, and to record a named owner for print-02 and cam-lobby so every asset maps to a real person.

glossary.CMDB (configuration management database): The official record of an organization's devices and who owns them.
glossary.Shadow IT: Devices or services used without IT's approval.
glossary.NAC (network access control): Technology that checks a device before letting it onto the network.
glossary.Clear / purge / destroy: Three levels of data removal: overwrite, make unrecoverable even in a lab, or physically destroy.
glossary.Degaussing: Erasing magnetic media with a strong magnet; it does nothing to SSDs (solid-state drives).
glossary.Legal hold: An order to keep data because of a lawsuit or investigation.
glossary.Certificate of destruction: Proof from a disposal vendor that the media was really destroyed.

briefing.talking_point: Reconciled an 8-asset CMDB with a discovery scan, finding 1 missing laptop, 3 unmanaged devices, 2 assets without owners and 2 unclassified, and approved 3 of 9 disposal requests while rejecting 6, including an SSD set for degaussing and media under legal hold.

lessons: Shadow IT devices nobody owns never get patched, monitored or wiped.
Degaussing an SSD: flash storage is not magnetic, so the data survives.
Overwriting an SSD: wear levelling leaves old blocks behind; use crypto-erase or destroy.
governance: Agents, models and API keys are assets: inventory them with an owner and a classification.
An unregistered AI agent or tool found in traffic is shadow IT: onboard it or block it.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring and
| privacy (with 5.1 data roles).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Deadlines here are configurable illustrations (GDPR-style 30 days / 72
| h), not legal advice; real law varies by local, regional, national and
| global scope.
|   • The controller decides why/how data is processed and answers data
| subject requests; a processor acts only on its instructions.
|   • Right to be forgotten is not absolute: a documented legal hold or
| retention obligation suspends erasure.
|   • A data inventory plus a retention schedule (minimum AND maximum
| periods) drives lawful keeping and destruction.
|   • Compliance monitoring: attestation and acknowledgement, internal and
| external audits, and automation of the checks.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Silently deleting data that is under legal hold (sanctions for
| spoliation).
|   • Keeping data 'just in case' long after its retention period (over-
| retention increases breach impact).
|   • A processor answering a subject request directly instead of forwarding
| it to the controller.
|   • Missing the regulator breach notification window while the
| investigation drags on.
|   • Annual policy acknowledgements tracked on paper and quietly expiring.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that handles DSRs must verify identity before disclosing
| or erasing anything.
|   • Agents need the data inventory too: training data and prompts are
| personal data with retention limits.
|   • Exceptions (holds) must be documented records an agent can check,
| never a free-text excuse it accepts.
|   • Automated compliance checks are monitoring, but attestation sign-off
| stays with an accountable human.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Internal reporting goes to management/board/compliance; external
| reporting goes to regulators, customers or auditors.
|   • Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage,
| loss of license, contractual impacts.
|   • Due diligence = investigate and verify; due care = act as a
| reasonable, prudent organisation would.
|   • Controller vs processor: the controller is accountable; the processor
| processes on the controller's behalf.
|   • Data subject = the person the data is about; right to be forgotten =
| erasure request.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring and
| privacy (with 5.1 data roles).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Deadlines here are configurable illustrations (GDPR-style 30 days / 72
| h), not legal advice; real law varies by local, regional, national and
| global scope.
|   • The controller decides why/how data is processed and answers data
| subject requests; a processor acts only on its instructions.
|   • Right to be forgotten is not absolute: a documented legal hold or
| retention obligation suspends erasure.
|   • A data inventory plus a retention schedule (minimum AND maximum
| periods) drives lawful keeping and destruction.
|   • Compliance monitoring: attestation and acknowledgement, internal and
| external audits, and automation of the checks.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Silently deleting data that is under legal hold (sanctions for
| spoliation).
|   • Keeping data 'just in case' long after its retention period (over-
| retention increases breach impact).
|   • A processor answering a subject request directly instead of forwarding
| it to the controller.
|   • Missing the regulator breach notification window while the
| investigation drags on.
|   • Annual policy acknowledgements tracked on paper and quietly expiring.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that handles DSRs must verify identity before disclosing
| or erasing anything.
|   • Agents need the data inventory too: training data and prompts are
| personal data with retention limits.
|   • Exceptions (holds) must be documented records an agent can check,
| never a free-text excuse it accepts.
|   • Automated compliance checks are monitoring, but attestation sign-off
| stays with an accountable human.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Internal reporting goes to management/board/compliance; external
| reporting goes to regulators, customers or auditors.
|   • Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage,
| loss of license, contractual impacts.
|   • Due diligence = investigate and verify; due care = act as a
| reasonable, prudent organisation would.
|   • Controller vs processor: the controller is accountable; the processor
| processes on the controller's behalf.
|   • Data subject = the person the data is about; right to be forgotten =
| erasure request.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring and
| privacy (with 5.1 data roles).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Deadlines here are configurable illustrations (GDPR-style 30 days / 72
| h), not legal advice; real law varies by local, regional, national and
| global scope.
|   • The controller decides why/how data is processed and answers data
| subject requests; a processor acts only on its instructions.
|   • Right to be forgotten is not absolute: a documented legal hold or
| retention obligation suspends erasure.
|   • A data inventory plus a retention schedule (minimum AND maximum
| periods) drives lawful keeping and destruction.
|   • Compliance monitoring: attestation and acknowledgement, internal and
| external audits, and automation of the checks.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Silently deleting data that is under legal hold (sanctions for
| spoliation).
|   • Keeping data 'just in case' long after its retention period (over-
| retention increases breach impact).
|   • A processor answering a subject request directly instead of forwarding
| it to the controller.
|   • Missing the regulator breach notification window while the
| investigation drags on.
|   • Annual policy acknowledgements tracked on paper and quietly expiring.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that handles DSRs must verify identity before disclosing
| or erasing anything.
|   • Agents need the data inventory too: training data and prompts are
| personal data with retention limits.
|   • Exceptions (holds) must be documented records an agent can check,
| never a free-text excuse it accepts.
|   • Automated compliance checks are monitoring, but attestation sign-off
| stays with an accountable human.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Internal reporting goes to management/board/compliance; external
| reporting goes to regulators, customers or auditors.
|   • Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage,
| loss of license, contractual impacts.
|   • Due diligence = investigate and verify; due care = act as a
| reasonable, prudent organisation would.
|   • Controller vs processor: the controller is accountable; the processor
| processes on the controller's behalf.
|   • Data subject = the person the data is about; right to be forgotten =
| erasure request.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring and
| privacy (with 5.1 data roles).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Deadlines here are configurable illustrations (GDPR-style 30 days / 72
| h), not legal advice; real law varies by local, regional, national and
| global scope.
|   • The controller decides why/how data is processed and answers data
| subject requests; a processor acts only on its instructions.
|   • Right to be forgotten is not absolute: a documented legal hold or
| retention obligation suspends erasure.
|   • A data inventory plus a retention schedule (minimum AND maximum
| periods) drives lawful keeping and destruction.
|   • Compliance monitoring: attestation and acknowledgement, internal and
| external audits, and automation of the checks.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Silently deleting data that is under legal hold (sanctions for
| spoliation).
|   • Keeping data 'just in case' long after its retention period (over-
| retention increases breach impact).
|   • A processor answering a subject request directly instead of forwarding
| it to the controller.
|   • Missing the regulator breach notification window while the
| investigation drags on.
|   • Annual policy acknowledgements tracked on paper and quietly expiring.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that handles DSRs must verify identity before disclosing
| or erasing anything.
|   • Agents need the data inventory too: training data and prompts are
| personal data with retention limits.
|   • Exceptions (holds) must be documented records an agent can check,
| never a free-text excuse it accepts.
|   • Automated compliance checks are monitoring, but attestation sign-off
| stays with an accountable human.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Internal reporting goes to management/board/compliance; external
| reporting goes to regulators, customers or auditors.
|   • Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage,
| loss of license, contractual impacts.
|   • Due diligence = investigate and verify; due care = act as a
| reasonable, prudent organisation would.
|   • Controller vs processor: the controller is accountable; the processor
| processes on the controller's behalf.
|   • Data subject = the person the data is about; right to be forgotten =
| erasure request.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring and
| privacy (with 5.1 data roles).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Deadlines here are configurable illustrations (GDPR-style 30 days / 72
| h), not legal advice; real law varies by local, regional, national and
| global scope.
|   • The controller decides why/how data is processed and answers data
| subject requests; a processor acts only on its instructions.
|   • Right to be forgotten is not absolute: a documented legal hold or
| retention obligation suspends erasure.
|   • A data inventory plus a retention schedule (minimum AND maximum
| periods) drives lawful keeping and destruction.
|   • Compliance monitoring: attestation and acknowledgement, internal and
| external audits, and automation of the checks.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Silently deleting data that is under legal hold (sanctions for
| spoliation).
|   • Keeping data 'just in case' long after its retention period (over-
| retention increases breach impact).
|   • A processor answering a subject request directly instead of forwarding
| it to the controller.
|   • Missing the regulator breach notification window while the
| investigation drags on.
|   • Annual policy acknowledgements tracked on paper and quietly expiring.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent that handles DSRs must verify identity before disclosing
| or erasing anything.
|   • Agents need the data inventory too: training data and prompts are
| personal data with retention limits.
|   • Exceptions (holds) must be documented records an agent can check,
| never a free-text excuse it accepts.
|   • Automated compliance checks are monitoring, but attestation sign-off
| stays with an accountable human.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Internal reporting goes to management/board/compliance; external
| reporting goes to regulators, customers or auditors.
|   • Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage,
| loss of license, contractual impacts.
|   • Due diligence = investigate and verify; due care = act as a
| reasonable, prudent organisation would.
|   • Controller vs processor: the controller is accountable; the processor
| processes on the controller's behalf.
|   • Data subject = the person the data is about; right to be forgotten =
| erasure request.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring and
| privacy (with 5.1 data roles).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Deadlines here are configurable illustrations (GDPR-style 30 days / 72
| h), not legal advice; real law varies by local, regional, national and
| global scope.
|   • The controller decides why/how data is processed and answers data
| subject requests; a processor acts only on its instructions.
|   • Right to be forgotten is not absolute: a documented legal hold or
| retention obligation suspends erasure.
|   • A data inventory plus a retention schedule (minimum AND maximum
| periods) drives lawful keeping and destruction.
|   • Compliance monitoring: attestation and acknowledgement, internal and
| external audits, and automation of the checks.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Silently deleting data that is under legal hold (sanctions for
| spoliation).
|   • Keeping data 'just in case' long after its retention period (over-
| retention increases breach impact).
|   • A processor answering a subject request directly instead of forwarding
| it to the controller.
|   • Missing the regulator breach notification window while the
| investigation drags on.
|   • Annual policy acknowledgements tracked on paper and quietly expiring.
|

|   • An AI agent that handles DSRs must verify identity before disclosing
| or erasing anything.
|   • Agents need the data inventory too: training data and prompts are
| personal data with retention limits.
|   • Exceptions (holds) must be documented records an agent can check,
| never a free-text excuse it accepts.
|   • Automated compliance checks are monitoring, but attestation sign-off
| stays with an accountable human.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Internal reporting goes to management/board/compliance; external
| reporting goes to regulators, customers or auditors.
|   • Consequences of non-compliance: fines, sanctions, reputational damage,
| loss of license, contractual impacts.
|   • Due diligence = investigate and verify; due care = act as a
| reasonable, prudent organisation would.
|   • Controller vs processor: the controller is accountable; the processor
| processes on the controller's behalf.
|   • Data subject = the person the data is about; right to be forgotten =
| erasure request.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Compliance & Privacy Obligations Tracker
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 5.4 Compliance reporting, consequences, monitoring, privacy (subject, controller vs processor, retention, right to be forgotten) · 5.1 Data roles: owner, controller, processor, custodian/steward

briefing.requested_by: Helen Marsh, Privacy and Compliance Manager
briefing.title: Thirteen privacy and compliance obligations: which are late?
briefing.situation: The compliance team is tracking 13 open items as of day 1000: customer requests to see, correct or delete their data, three data breaches, data-retention cases and signed attestations. Some deadlines have already passed, and one customer request was sent to our payroll provider instead of to us. Leadership needs a status report and to know which items must be reported outside the company.
your_task: Apply each item's deadline rule and mark it COMPLIANT, AT_RISK, NON_COMPLIANT or EXEMPT.
Check data-subject requests for identity verification and correct routing between controller and processor.
Check breach notices against the 72-hour regulator deadline and whether affected people were told.
Check retention cases for data kept too long or destroyed too early, allowing for legal holds, and produce the summary report.
briefing.why_it_matters: Late breach notices and missed privacy deadlines bring fines, and an expired attestation can cost a customer contract or a license. Acting on a deletion request without verifying identity can hand someone else's data to an impostor.
done_when: All 13 items have a status, a rule and a consequence.
The report shows COMPLIANT 2, AT_RISK 2, NON_COMPLIANT 7, EXEMPT 2, and lists the 4 items needing external reporting.

DSR-5 is routed to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) team to verify the requester's identity before any erasure, and for BR-3 (credential stuffing) affected customers are notified and IAM confirms the compromised accounts were reset.

glossary.DSR (data subject request): A person's request to see, correct or delete the data a company holds about them.
glossary.Data controller: The organization that decides why and how personal data is used.
glossary.Data processor: A company that handles personal data only on the controller's instructions.
glossary.Right to be forgotten: A person's right to have their data deleted, unless a law or legal hold requires keeping it.
glossary.Retention period: The minimum and maximum time a type of record must be kept.
glossary.Attestation: A signed statement that controls are in place, often owed to customers or auditors.
glossary.Credential stuffing: Trying usernames and passwords stolen from other sites on our login page.

briefing.talking_point: Tracked 13 privacy and compliance obligations and found 7 non-compliant, including a breach notice 28 hours late, audit logs destroyed 225 days early and an erasure request with no identity verification, with 4 items needing external reporting.

lessons: Silently deleting data that is under legal hold (sanctions for spoliation).
Keeping data 'just in case' long after its retention period (over-retention increases breach impact).
A processor answering a subject request directly instead of forwarding it to the controller.
governance: An AI agent that handles DSRs must verify identity before disclosing or erasing anything.
Agents need the data inventory too: training data and prompts are personal data with retention limits.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

| Objective: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation,
| internal/external audits, penetration testing and reconnaissance.
