| Key Concepts
|   • Rules of engagement set scope, timing, allowed and prohibited
| techniques, and an emergency contact; signed authorization comes first.
|   • Known, partially known and unknown environments describe how much the
| testers are told beforehand.
|   • Passive recon uses public sources (OSINT, WHOIS, certificate logs);
| active recon sends traffic to the target (port scans, banner grabs).
|   • Offensive = red team, defensive = blue team, integrated = purple team;
| physical tests target doors, badges and guards.
|   • Internal audits (compliance, audit committee, self-assessment) differ
| from external ones (regulatory exam, independent third-party audit,
| attestation).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Scanning an IP that 'looked like ours' but belonged to a neighbour:
| unauthorised access, whatever the intent.
|   • Running a DoS test in business hours with no emergency contact,
| causing a real outage.
|   • Treating a team's self-assessment as if it gave an independent
| opinion.
|   • Calling an active scan 'passive' to slip outside the agreed testing
| window.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI pentest agent should call an RoE gate before every action, not
| once at the start of the engagement.
|   • Deny by default: an unknown technique or an unparseable target is
| BLOCKED, never guessed.
|   • The agent's own label (e.g. 'passive') is untrusted; the gate
| reclassifies the technique from its catalogue.
|   • Out-of-scope lists win over in-scope ranges, and every decision is
| logged with its reasons for the final report.
|

|   • 'Testers are given network diagrams and credentials' = known
| environment; 'given nothing' = unknown environment.
|   • OSINT, WHOIS and social-media research = passive reconnaissance; ping
| sweeps and port scans = active.
|   • Attestation = an independent party formally vouches for controls (e.g.
| a SOC 2 report).
|   • Audit committee oversees internal audit; regulators perform
| examinations; an outside auditor gives independence.
|   • Purple team = integrated testing where red and blue teams share
| findings.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation,
| internal/external audits, penetration testing and reconnaissance.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Rules of engagement set scope, timing, allowed and prohibited
| techniques, and an emergency contact; signed authorization comes first.
|   • Known, partially known and unknown environments describe how much the
| testers are told beforehand.
|   • Passive recon uses public sources (OSINT, WHOIS, certificate logs);
| active recon sends traffic to the target (port scans, banner grabs).
|   • Offensive = red team, defensive = blue team, integrated = purple team;
| physical tests target doors, badges and guards.
|   • Internal audits (compliance, audit committee, self-assessment) differ
| from external ones (regulatory exam, independent third-party audit,
| attestation).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Scanning an IP that 'looked like ours' but belonged to a neighbour:
| unauthorised access, whatever the intent.
|   • Running a DoS test in business hours with no emergency contact,
| causing a real outage.
|   • Treating a team's self-assessment as if it gave an independent
| opinion.
|   • Calling an active scan 'passive' to slip outside the agreed testing
| window.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI pentest agent should call an RoE gate before every action, not
| once at the start of the engagement.
|   • Deny by default: an unknown technique or an unparseable target is
| BLOCKED, never guessed.
|   • The agent's own label (e.g. 'passive') is untrusted; the gate
| reclassifies the technique from its catalogue.
|   • Out-of-scope lists win over in-scope ranges, and every decision is
| logged with its reasons for the final report.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Testers are given network diagrams and credentials' = known
| environment; 'given nothing' = unknown environment.
|   • OSINT, WHOIS and social-media research = passive reconnaissance; ping
| sweeps and port scans = active.
|   • Attestation = an independent party formally vouches for controls (e.g.
| a SOC 2 report).
|   • Audit committee oversees internal audit; regulators perform
| examinations; an outside auditor gives independence.
|   • Purple team = integrated testing where red and blue teams share
| findings.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation,
| internal/external audits, penetration testing and reconnaissance.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Rules of engagement set scope, timing, allowed and prohibited
| techniques, and an emergency contact; signed authorization comes first.
|   • Known, partially known and unknown environments describe how much the
| testers are told beforehand.
|   • Passive recon uses public sources (OSINT, WHOIS, certificate logs);
| active recon sends traffic to the target (port scans, banner grabs).
|   • Offensive = red team, defensive = blue team, integrated = purple team;
| physical tests target doors, badges and guards.
|   • Internal audits (compliance, audit committee, self-assessment) differ
| from external ones (regulatory exam, independent third-party audit,
| attestation).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Scanning an IP that 'looked like ours' but belonged to a neighbour:
| unauthorised access, whatever the intent.
|   • Running a DoS test in business hours with no emergency contact,
| causing a real outage.
|   • Treating a team's self-assessment as if it gave an independent
| opinion.
|   • Calling an active scan 'passive' to slip outside the agreed testing
| window.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI pentest agent should call an RoE gate before every action, not
| once at the start of the engagement.
|   • Deny by default: an unknown technique or an unparseable target is
| BLOCKED, never guessed.
|   • The agent's own label (e.g. 'passive') is untrusted; the gate
| reclassifies the technique from its catalogue.
|   • Out-of-scope lists win over in-scope ranges, and every decision is
| logged with its reasons for the final report.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Testers are given network diagrams and credentials' = known
| environment; 'given nothing' = unknown environment.
|   • OSINT, WHOIS and social-media research = passive reconnaissance; ping
| sweeps and port scans = active.
|   • Attestation = an independent party formally vouches for controls (e.g.
| a SOC 2 report).
|   • Audit committee oversees internal audit; regulators perform
| examinations; an outside auditor gives independence.
|   • Purple team = integrated testing where red and blue teams share
| findings.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation,
| internal/external audits, penetration testing and reconnaissance.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Rules of engagement set scope, timing, allowed and prohibited
| techniques, and an emergency contact; signed authorization comes first.
|   • Known, partially known and unknown environments describe how much the
| testers are told beforehand.
|   • Passive recon uses public sources (OSINT, WHOIS, certificate logs);
| active recon sends traffic to the target (port scans, banner grabs).
|   • Offensive = red team, defensive = blue team, integrated = purple team;
| physical tests target doors, badges and guards.
|   • Internal audits (compliance, audit committee, self-assessment) differ
| from external ones (regulatory exam, independent third-party audit,
| attestation).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Scanning an IP that 'looked like ours' but belonged to a neighbour:
| unauthorised access, whatever the intent.
|   • Running a DoS test in business hours with no emergency contact,
| causing a real outage.
|   • Treating a team's self-assessment as if it gave an independent
| opinion.
|   • Calling an active scan 'passive' to slip outside the agreed testing
| window.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI pentest agent should call an RoE gate before every action, not
| once at the start of the engagement.
|   • Deny by default: an unknown technique or an unparseable target is
| BLOCKED, never guessed.
|   • The agent's own label (e.g. 'passive') is untrusted; the gate
| reclassifies the technique from its catalogue.
|   • Out-of-scope lists win over in-scope ranges, and every decision is
| logged with its reasons for the final report.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Testers are given network diagrams and credentials' = known
| environment; 'given nothing' = unknown environment.
|   • OSINT, WHOIS and social-media research = passive reconnaissance; ping
| sweeps and port scans = active.
|   • Attestation = an independent party formally vouches for controls (e.g.
| a SOC 2 report).
|   • Audit committee oversees internal audit; regulators perform
| examinations; an outside auditor gives independence.
|   • Purple team = integrated testing where red and blue teams share
| findings.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Assessment needs
ID    Driver              Independent?  Assessment type                Internal/external

AN-1  compliance_review   no            INTERNAL_AUDIT                 internal
AN-2  regulator_requires  yes           REGULATORY_EXAMINATION         external

  • AN-1: checking adherence to internal policy and law is the internal audit compliance function
  • AN-2: a regulator mandates it, so the regulator (or its examiners) performs an external examination
  • AN-3: a regulator mandates it, so the regulator (or its examiners) performs an external examination
  • AN-4: checking adherence to internal policy and law is the internal audit compliance function; independence required, so INTERNAL_AUDIT is not enough → INDEPENDENT_THIRD_PARTY_AUDIT

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation,
| internal/external audits, penetration testing and reconnaissance.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Rules of engagement set scope, timing, allowed and prohibited
| techniques, and an emergency contact; signed authorization comes first.
|   • Known, partially known and unknown environments describe how much the
| testers are told beforehand.
|   • Passive recon uses public sources (OSINT, WHOIS, certificate logs);
| active recon sends traffic to the target (port scans, banner grabs).
|   • Offensive = red team, defensive = blue team, integrated = purple team;
| physical tests target doors, badges and guards.
|   • Internal audits (compliance, audit committee, self-assessment) differ
| from external ones (regulatory exam, independent third-party audit,
| attestation).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Scanning an IP that 'looked like ours' but belonged to a neighbour:
| unauthorised access, whatever the intent.
|   • Running a DoS test in business hours with no emergency contact,
| causing a real outage.
|   • Treating a team's self-assessment as if it gave an independent
| opinion.
|   • Calling an active scan 'passive' to slip outside the agreed testing
| window.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI pentest agent should call an RoE gate before every action, not
| once at the start of the engagement.
|   • Deny by default: an unknown technique or an unparseable target is
| BLOCKED, never guessed.
|   • The agent's own label (e.g. 'passive') is untrusted; the gate
| reclassifies the technique from its catalogue.
|   • Out-of-scope lists win over in-scope ranges, and every decision is
| logged with its reasons for the final report.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Testers are given network diagrams and credentials' = known
| environment; 'given nothing' = unknown environment.
|   • OSINT, WHOIS and social-media research = passive reconnaissance; ping
| sweeps and port scans = active.
|   • Attestation = an independent party formally vouches for controls (e.g.
| a SOC 2 report).
|   • Audit committee oversees internal audit; regulators perform
| examinations; an outside auditor gives independence.
|   • Purple team = integrated testing where red and blue teams share
| findings.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation,
| internal/external audits, penetration testing and reconnaissance.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Rules of engagement set scope, timing, allowed and prohibited
| techniques, and an emergency contact; signed authorization comes first.
|   • Known, partially known and unknown environments describe how much the
| testers are told beforehand.
|   • Passive recon uses public sources (OSINT, WHOIS, certificate logs);
| active recon sends traffic to the target (port scans, banner grabs).
|   • Offensive = red team, defensive = blue team, integrated = purple team;
| physical tests target doors, badges and guards.
|   • Internal audits (compliance, audit committee, self-assessment) differ
| from external ones (regulatory exam, independent third-party audit,
| attestation).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Scanning an IP that 'looked like ours' but belonged to a neighbour:
| unauthorised access, whatever the intent.
|   • Running a DoS test in business hours with no emergency contact,
| causing a real outage.
|   • Treating a team's self-assessment as if it gave an independent
| opinion.
|   • Calling an active scan 'passive' to slip outside the agreed testing
| window.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI pentest agent should call an RoE gate before every action, not
| once at the start of the engagement.
|   • Deny by default: an unknown technique or an unparseable target is
| BLOCKED, never guessed.
|   • The agent's own label (e.g. 'passive') is untrusted; the gate
| reclassifies the technique from its catalogue.
|   • Out-of-scope lists win over in-scope ranges, and every decision is
| logged with its reasons for the final report.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Testers are given network diagrams and credentials' = known
| environment; 'given nothing' = unknown environment.
|   • OSINT, WHOIS and social-media research = passive reconnaissance; ping
| sweeps and port scans = active.
|   • Attestation = an independent party formally vouches for controls (e.g.
| a SOC 2 report).
|   • Audit committee oversees internal audit; regulators perform
| examinations; an outside auditor gives independence.
|   • Purple team = integrated testing where red and blue teams share
| findings.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Penetration Test Rules-of-Engagement Gate & Audit Planner
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 5.5 Audits and assessments: attestation, internal/external, penetration testing, reconnaissance · 4.3 Penetration testing · 5.3 Rules of engagement

briefing.title: Check ten planned pen-test actions against the signed rules of engagement
briefing.situation: Our client signed rules of engagement for a 10-day penetration test, listing the in-scope networks, the excluded ones, allowed testing hours and banned techniques. Ten test actions are planned, some by a human tester and some by an AI testing agent. The client also needs five upcoming audits matched to the right type of assessment.
your_task: Check each planned action is signed off, inside the authorized dates and inside an in-scope target range.
Check the technique is allowed and the time is inside the testing window, with the stated exemption for passive research.
Mark each action ALLOW, BLOCK or NEEDS_APPROVAL, and name who must approve.
Match each audit need to the right assessment type, and whether it is internal or external.
briefing.why_it_matters: Testing outside the signed scope or hours is unauthorized access, which can break the law and take down a client's systems. Picking the wrong kind of audit can fail a regulator or customer requirement.
done_when: All 10 actions have a decision and a reason (2 allowed, 7 blocked, 1 needing approval).
The web-app test is held until the CISO gives written approval.
All 5 assessment needs are matched to a type, and the IAM team confirms the AI agent and tester accounts are disabled after day 10.

glossary.Penetration test: An authorized, simulated attack to find weaknesses before real attackers do.
glossary.Rules of engagement (RoE): The signed agreement that sets what testers may touch, how and when.
glossary.Scope: The list of systems that may be tested; anything else is off limits.
glossary.Passive vs active reconnaissance: Passive research reads public sources only; active research sends traffic to the target.
glossary.Attestation (SOC 2): An independent auditor's report on a company's controls.
glossary.CISO: Chief information security officer, the senior security leader.

briefing.talking_point: Gated 10 planned penetration-test actions against signed rules of engagement, allowing 2, blocking 7 for scope, time window, banned or unknown technique and expired authorization, and holding 1 for CISO approval, then matched 5 audit needs to the right assessment type.

lessons: Scanning an IP that 'looked like ours' but belonged to a neighbour: unauthorised access, whatever the intent.
Running a DoS test in business hours with no emergency contact, causing a real outage.
Treating a team's self-assessment as if it gave an independent opinion.
governance: An AI pentest agent should call an RoE gate before every action, not once at the start of the engagement.
Deny by default: an unknown technique or an unparseable target is BLOCKED, never guessed.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.

| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.

| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.

| your early-warning sensor.

| recognises a phish.

| untrained.

| evidence disappears.

|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.

| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.

| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.

|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness practices: phishing campaigns,
| anomalous behaviour, training, reporting.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Phishing campaigns (simulations) measure click, credential-submission
| and report rates; the report rate matters most.
|   • Anomalous behaviour is risky (deliberate rule-bending), unexpected
| (out of pattern) or unintentional (honest mistake).
|   • Training topics: policy/handbooks, situational awareness, insider
| threat, passwords, removable media and cables, social engineering, OPSEC,
| hybrid/remote work.
|   • Initial training happens at onboarding; recurring training keeps it
| current. Reporting and monitoring track both.
|   • A program is developed (goals, audience, content), executed (delivery,
| simulations) and measured against KPIs.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is
| your early-warning sensor.
|   • One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually
| recognises a phish.
|   • Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although
| BEC targets high-risk roles.
|   • Treating a missing training record as 'probably done' instead of
| untrained.
|   • Sending insider-threat suspicions to the user's manager first, so
| evidence disappears.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one,
| not just say 'safe'.
|   • Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow
| instructions found inside an email.
|   • An agent may assign micro-training automatically, but escalation and
| insider-threat referral need a human.
|   • Log every classification with the policy version so behaviour verdicts
| can be audited and contested.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not
| click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
|   • Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request
| from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
|   • 'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable
| media training (baiting).
|   • Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline,
| unintentional = accident: know the three words.
|   • Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based
| training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Security Awareness Program Analyzer
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 5.6 Security awareness: phishing campaigns, anomalous behaviour, training, reporting · 2.2 Phishing/BEC vectors

briefing.requested_by: Natalie Brooks, Security Awareness Program Lead
briefing.title: Phishing test PH-2026-Q4 results: who clicked, who gave up a password, what next
briefing.situation: We ran a simulated phishing email for 12 employees in Finance, Engineering, Sales and HR. Two people entered their passwords on the fake page, and three clicked the link. We also have five unusual behaviour reports, like an admin stopping security software, and four real emails users forwarded for a verdict.
your_task: Give each employee a follow-up action based on their result, role risk, repeat failures and training record.
Calculate click, password-entry and report rates by department and for the whole program, against targets.
Classify the five behaviour reports and pick a response and a technical control for each.
Score the four forwarded emails on phishing signs and mark each one REPORT_AS_PHISHING or LIKELY_SAFE.
briefing.why_it_matters: A password typed into a fake page is a real account compromise until it is reset. Departments that handle money, like Finance, are the main targets for invoice and payment fraud.
done_when: All 12 employees have an action and the rule that triggered it.
Department and program metrics are reported, with Finance, HR and Sales flagged.
The two password submitters (E03, E08) are sent to the Identity and Access Management (IAM) team for a forced password reset, session revocation and a check of multi-factor authentication (MFA).
Both risky behaviours (B1, B4) are referred to the insider-threat team.

glossary.Phishing simulation: A safe, fake phishing email sent to staff to measure and train their responses.
glossary.Credential submission: Typing a username and password into the fake page; in real life, the account would be compromised.
glossary.Report rate: The share of people who reported the email to security.
glossary.BEC (business email compromise): A scam that uses fake or hijacked business email to get payments or data.
glossary.Typosquatting: Using a look-alike domain, like examp1e.com, to trick people.
glossary.UEBA: User and entity behaviour analytics: tools that flag activity unusual for a person or device.

briefing.talking_point: Analyzed a 12-person phishing test with a 41.7% click rate and 16.7% password-entry rate, flagged 3 of 4 departments, sent the 2 compromised users to IAM for forced resets and session revocation, and flagged 2 of 4 forwarded emails as phishing.

results: E01: REPORTED, NONE, e02: CLICKED, REMEDIAL_TRAINING, e03: COMPROMISED, ESCALATE_TO_MANAGER, e04: REPORTED, NONE, e05: PASSED, NONE, e06: REPORTED, NONE, e07: CLICKED, ESCALATE_TO_MANAGER, e08: COMPROMISED, REMEDIAL_TRAINING, e09: PASSED, REMEDIAL_TRAINING, e10: REPORTED, MICRO_TRAINING, e11: NO_DATA, REMEDIAL_TRAINING, e12: CLICKED, MICRO_TRAINING
5 total: Risky 2, Unintentional 1, Unexpected 1, Not anomalous 1
4 total: Report as phishing 2, Likely safe 2
lessons: Punishing every click: people stop reporting, and the report rate is your early-warning sensor.
One annual video and no simulations: no data on who actually recognises a phish.
Same thresholds for the finance clerk and the payroll admin, although BEC targets high-risk roles.
governance: An AI mail triage agent should score indicators and explain each one, not just say 'safe'.
Message bodies are untrusted input: the agent must never follow instructions found inside an email.
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Conditional access, MFA, least privilege, PAM (JIT)
| · 1.2 Adaptive identity, PE/PEP · 2.4 Impossible travel.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Conditional access is if-then policy: IF user, app, risk, device,
| location and client app match, THEN block or require controls.
|   • All applicable policies are combined: any block wins, otherwise every
| required control from every policy must be met.
|   • Exclusions beat inclusions; report-only mode logs what a policy would
| do before you enforce it.
|   • PAM: just-in-time permissions replace standing admin roles; password
| vaulting and ephemeral credentials limit what can be stolen.
|   • Same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access / PIM (SC-300),
| described here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do
| MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
|   • Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits
| the moment one account is phished.
|   • Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts
| were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
|   • Assuming 'no policy matched' means 'blocked': without a deny-by-
| default rule it means allowed with a password only.
|   • Letting requesters approve their own privileged activation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for
| one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
|   • An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload
| identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
|   • An agent may draft activation requests, but a human approver who is
| not the requester must approve high-privilege roles.
|   • Run new agent access policies in report-only mode first and review the
| 'would have blocked' log.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Access changes based on location, device health and risk' =
| conditional / context-aware access, adaptive identity.
|   • 'Admin rights granted only for the time needed, then revoked' = just-
| in-time permissions (PAM).
|   • 'Credentials that exist for one session' = ephemeral credentials;
| 'checked out from a vault' = password vaulting.
|   • Two logins from distant countries minutes apart = impossible travel
| (an indicator of compromised credentials).
|   • Policy Engine decides, Policy Enforcement Point enforces; conditional
| access is the policy engine for sign-ins.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| (an indicator of compromised credentials).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Conditional access, MFA, least privilege, PAM (JIT)
| · 1.2 Adaptive identity, PE/PEP · 2.4 Impossible travel.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Conditional access is if-then policy: IF user, app, risk, device,
| location and client app match, THEN block or require controls.
|   • All applicable policies are combined: any block wins, otherwise every
| required control from every policy must be met.
|   • Exclusions beat inclusions; report-only mode logs what a policy would
| do before you enforce it.
|   • PAM: just-in-time permissions replace standing admin roles; password
| vaulting and ephemeral credentials limit what can be stolen.
|   • Same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access / PIM (SC-300),
| described here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do
| MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
|   • Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits
| the moment one account is phished.
|   • Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts
| were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
|   • Assuming 'no policy matched' means 'blocked': without a deny-by-
| default rule it means allowed with a password only.
|   • Letting requesters approve their own privileged activation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for
| one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
|   • An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload
| identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
|   • An agent may draft activation requests, but a human approver who is
| not the requester must approve high-privilege roles.
|   • Run new agent access policies in report-only mode first and review the
| 'would have blocked' log.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Access changes based on location, device health and risk' =
| conditional / context-aware access, adaptive identity.
|   • 'Admin rights granted only for the time needed, then revoked' = just-
| in-time permissions (PAM).
|   • 'Credentials that exist for one session' = ephemeral credentials;
| 'checked out from a vault' = password vaulting.
|   • Two logins from distant countries minutes apart = impossible travel
| (an indicator of compromised credentials).
|   • Policy Engine decides, Policy Enforcement Point enforces; conditional
| access is the policy engine for sign-ins.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Conditional access, MFA, least privilege, PAM (JIT)
| · 1.2 Adaptive identity, PE/PEP · 2.4 Impossible travel.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Conditional access is if-then policy: IF user, app, risk, device,
| location and client app match, THEN block or require controls.
|   • All applicable policies are combined: any block wins, otherwise every
| required control from every policy must be met.
|   • Exclusions beat inclusions; report-only mode logs what a policy would
| do before you enforce it.
|   • PAM: just-in-time permissions replace standing admin roles; password
| vaulting and ephemeral credentials limit what can be stolen.
|   • Same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access / PIM (SC-300),
| described here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do
| MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
|   • Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits
| the moment one account is phished.
|   • Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts
| were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
|   • Assuming 'no policy matched' means 'blocked': without a deny-by-
| default rule it means allowed with a password only.
|   • Letting requesters approve their own privileged activation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for
| one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
|   • An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload
| identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
|   • An agent may draft activation requests, but a human approver who is
| not the requester must approve high-privilege roles.
|   • Run new agent access policies in report-only mode first and review the
| 'would have blocked' log.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Access changes based on location, device health and risk' =
| conditional / context-aware access, adaptive identity.
|   • 'Admin rights granted only for the time needed, then revoked' = just-
| in-time permissions (PAM).
|   • 'Credentials that exist for one session' = ephemeral credentials;
| 'checked out from a vault' = password vaulting.
|   • Two logins from distant countries minutes apart = impossible travel
| (an indicator of compromised credentials).
|   • Policy Engine decides, Policy Enforcement Point enforces; conditional
| access is the policy engine for sign-ins.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Conditional access, MFA, least privilege, PAM (JIT)
| · 1.2 Adaptive identity, PE/PEP · 2.4 Impossible travel.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Conditional access is if-then policy: IF user, app, risk, device,
| location and client app match, THEN block or require controls.
|   • All applicable policies are combined: any block wins, otherwise every
| required control from every policy must be met.
|   • Exclusions beat inclusions; report-only mode logs what a policy would
| do before you enforce it.
|   • PAM: just-in-time permissions replace standing admin roles; password
| vaulting and ephemeral credentials limit what can be stolen.
|   • Same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access / PIM (SC-300),
| described here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do
| MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
|   • Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits
| the moment one account is phished.
|   • Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts
| were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
|   • Assuming 'no policy matched' means 'blocked': without a deny-by-
| default rule it means allowed with a password only.
|   • Letting requesters approve their own privileged activation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for
| one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
|   • An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload
| identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
|   • An agent may draft activation requests, but a human approver who is
| not the requester must approve high-privilege roles.
|   • Run new agent access policies in report-only mode first and review the
| 'would have blocked' log.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Access changes based on location, device health and risk' =
| conditional / context-aware access, adaptive identity.
|   • 'Admin rights granted only for the time needed, then revoked' = just-
| in-time permissions (PAM).
|   • 'Credentials that exist for one session' = ephemeral credentials;
| 'checked out from a vault' = password vaulting.
|   • Two logins from distant countries minutes apart = impossible travel
| (an indicator of compromised credentials).
|   • Policy Engine decides, Policy Enforcement Point enforces; conditional
| access is the policy engine for sign-ins.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Conditional access, MFA, least privilege, PAM (JIT)
| · 1.2 Adaptive identity, PE/PEP · 2.4 Impossible travel.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Conditional access is if-then policy: IF user, app, risk, device,
| location and client app match, THEN block or require controls.
|   • All applicable policies are combined: any block wins, otherwise every
| required control from every policy must be met.
|   • Exclusions beat inclusions; report-only mode logs what a policy would
| do before you enforce it.
|   • PAM: just-in-time permissions replace standing admin roles; password
| vaulting and ephemeral credentials limit what can be stolen.
|   • Same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access / PIM (SC-300),
| described here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do
| MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
|   • Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits
| the moment one account is phished.
|   • Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts
| were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
|   • Assuming 'no policy matched' means 'blocked': without a deny-by-
| default rule it means allowed with a password only.
|   • Letting requesters approve their own privileged activation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for
| one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
|   • An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload
| identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
|   • An agent may draft activation requests, but a human approver who is
| not the requester must approve high-privilege roles.
|   • Run new agent access policies in report-only mode first and review the
| 'would have blocked' log.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Access changes based on location, device health and risk' =
| conditional / context-aware access, adaptive identity.
|   • 'Admin rights granted only for the time needed, then revoked' = just-
| in-time permissions (PAM).
|   • 'Credentials that exist for one session' = ephemeral credentials;
| 'checked out from a vault' = password vaulting.
|   • Two logins from distant countries minutes apart = impossible travel
| (an indicator of compromised credentials).
|   • Policy Engine decides, Policy Enforcement Point enforces; conditional
| access is the policy engine for sign-ins.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Conditional access, MFA, least privilege, PAM (JIT)
| · 1.2 Adaptive identity, PE/PEP · 2.4 Impossible travel.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Conditional access is if-then policy: IF user, app, risk, device,
| location and client app match, THEN block or require controls.
|   • All applicable policies are combined: any block wins, otherwise every
| required control from every policy must be met.
|   • Exclusions beat inclusions; report-only mode logs what a policy would
| do before you enforce it.
|   • PAM: just-in-time permissions replace standing admin roles; password
| vaulting and ephemeral credentials limit what can be stolen.
|   • Same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access / PIM (SC-300),
| described here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do
| MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
|   • Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits
| the moment one account is phished.
|   • Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts
| were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
|   • Assuming 'no policy matched' means 'blocked': without a deny-by-
| default rule it means allowed with a password only.
|   • Letting requesters approve their own privileged activation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for
| one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
|   • An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload
| identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
|   • An agent may draft activation requests, but a human approver who is
| not the requester must approve high-privilege roles.
|   • Run new agent access policies in report-only mode first and review the
| 'would have blocked' log.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Access changes based on location, device health and risk' =
| conditional / context-aware access, adaptive identity.
|   • 'Admin rights granted only for the time needed, then revoked' = just-
| in-time permissions (PAM).
|   • 'Credentials that exist for one session' = ephemeral credentials;
| 'checked out from a vault' = password vaulting.
|   • Two logins from distant countries minutes apart = impossible travel
| (an indicator of compromised credentials).
|   • Policy Engine decides, Policy Enforcement Point enforces; conditional
| access is the policy engine for sign-ins.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Conditional access, MFA, least privilege, PAM (JIT)
| · 1.2 Adaptive identity, PE/PEP · 2.4 Impossible travel.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Conditional access is if-then policy: IF user, app, risk, device,
| location and client app match, THEN block or require controls.
|   • All applicable policies are combined: any block wins, otherwise every
| required control from every policy must be met.
|   • Exclusions beat inclusions; report-only mode logs what a policy would
| do before you enforce it.
|   • PAM: just-in-time permissions replace standing admin roles; password
| vaulting and ephemeral credentials limit what can be stolen.
|   • Same model as Microsoft Entra Conditional Access / PIM (SC-300),
| described here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do
| MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
|   • Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits
| the moment one account is phished.
|   • Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts
| were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
|   • Assuming 'no policy matched' means 'blocked': without a deny-by-
| default rule it means allowed with a password only.
|   • Letting requesters approve their own privileged activation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for
| one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
|   • An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload
| identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
|   • An agent may draft activation requests, but a human approver who is
| not the requester must approve high-privilege roles.
|   • Run new agent access policies in report-only mode first and review the
| 'would have blocked' log.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Access changes based on location, device health and risk' =
| conditional / context-aware access, adaptive identity.
|   • 'Admin rights granted only for the time needed, then revoked' = just-
| in-time permissions (PAM).
|   • 'Credentials that exist for one session' = ephemeral credentials;
| 'checked out from a vault' = password vaulting.
|   • Two logins from distant countries minutes apart = impossible travel
| (an indicator of compromised credentials).
|   • Policy Engine decides, Policy Enforcement Point enforces; conditional
| access is the policy engine for sign-ins.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

case_study.title: Conditional Access & Just-in-Time Privileged Access
case_study.objectives: SY0-701 4.6 IAM: MFA, conditional access, least privilege, PAM (JIT, vaulting, ephemeral credentials) · 1.2 Zero trust adaptive identity, policy engine/enforcement · 2.4 Impossible travel, concurrent sessions

briefing.requested_by: Renee Holloway, IT Audit Manager, Prairie Wind Credit Union
briefing.title: Check our sign-in rules and who holds admin rights before the identity audit
briefing.situation: Auditors want proof that our sign-in rules work and that nobody keeps admin rights they do not need. We have eight Conditional Access policies (if-then rules that decide what a sign-in needs), a log of 13 recent sign-ins, a list of who holds admin roles, and seven requests from staff to switch on an admin role for a short time. Some rules may be missing, and two people have had full admin rights for years.
your_task: Run each sign-in through every policy and record the outcome: allowed, allowed after MFA (multifactor authentication), stopped for MFA, or blocked.
Note what the report-only (test-mode) policy would have done, without enforcing it.
Flag sensitive apps that no policy protects, and suspicious patterns such as impossible travel.
Review admin role assignments: flag permanent admin rights and check the two emergency (break-glass) accounts.
Approve, hold for approval, or deny each request to switch on an admin role, using the role's rules.
briefing.why_it_matters: One stolen password on an account that always has admin rights can hand an attacker the whole company. Sign-in rules that silently miss an app, or old email protocols that skip MFA, are how most account takeovers start.
done_when: Every sign-in has an outcome and the list of policies that applied, with a reason.
Coverage gaps, impossible travel and the report-only results are written up for the auditor.
Each permanent admin assignment has a fix (make it eligible, just-in-time) and the break-glass findings are logged.
Every role activation request has a decision with the rule that drove it.

glossary.Conditional Access: If-then sign-in rules: if this user, app, location, device or risk matches, then block or require extra checks.
glossary.MFA (multifactor authentication): Proving who you are with two or more kinds of proof, such as a password plus a phone prompt.
glossary.Report-only mode: A policy that is tested and logged but not enforced, so you can see its effect before switching it on.
glossary.Legacy authentication: Old email sign-in methods (IMAP, POP, basic SMTP) that cannot ask for MFA.
glossary.Just-in-time (JIT) access: Admin rights switched on only when needed, for a few hours, then removed automatically.
glossary.Standing privilege: Admin rights that are switched on all the time, whether or not they are being used.
glossary.Break-glass account: An emergency admin account kept out of normal sign-in rules so you are never locked out, and watched closely.
glossary.Impossible travel: Two sign-ins for one person from places too far apart to travel between in the time shown.

briefing.talking_point: Evaluated 13 sign-ins against 8 Conditional Access policies (4 blocked, 3 allowed after MFA, 2 stopped for MFA), caught an impossible-travel sign-in and an unprotected payroll app, flagged 2 permanent admin assignments and a mis-configured break-glass account, and decided 7 just-in-time admin requests (2 approved, 1 sent for approval, 4 denied).

results: 13 total: Block 4, Allow 4, Allow after MFA 3, Interrupted MFA required 2
5 total: Standing privilege 2, Break glass ok 1, Break glass finding 1, Time bound 1
lessons: Leaving legacy authentication (IMAP/POP/basic SMTP) open: it cannot do MFA, so password spraying bypasses MFA policies.
Permanent Global Administrator assignments that an attacker inherits the moment one account is phished.
Locking everyone out with a new policy because break-glass accounts were not excluded (or testing without report-only).
governance: Give AI agents eligible, time-boxed roles: they activate a scope for one task and lose it automatically afterwards.
An agent's own identity should face conditional access too (workload identity, trusted location, short-lived tokens).
case_study.note: Simulated lab with fictional people, systems and data, built with the open-source IdentityOps Lab (practice aligned to the CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 exam objectives). Results come from running the lab's engine on its sample scenario.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Provisioning/de-provisioning and attestation · 5.1
| Owners · 4.2 Account inventory.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • HR is the authoritative source; aggregation pulls every app's
| accounts, correlation links each to a person.
|   • An entitlement is one permission; an access profile bundles one app's
| entitlements; a role bundles profiles for a job.
|   • Orphaned, dormant and terminated-but-enabled accounts are de-
| provisioning failures an attacker can reuse.
|   • Access certification (attestation) has the manager or entitlement
| owner re-approve access on a schedule.
|   • These are the same concepts SailPoint and Entra ID Governance use,
| shown here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaver process disables the directory account but not the ERP or SaaS
| accounts.
|   • Service accounts created for a project with no owner, still privileged
| years later.
|   • Reviewers approving everything in seconds: the certification becomes
| paperwork, not a control.
|   • Treating an undecided item as 'keep' so access survives because nobody
| looked at it.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent can aggregate and correlate accounts, but revoking access
| stays a human-approved, logged change.
|   • Give an agent a service account with a named human owner and least
| privilege, then certify it like any other.
|   • Agents that recommend approve/revoke must show reasons; a reviewer who
| just accepts them is rubber-stamping.
|   • Treat comments and attributes in app exports as untrusted data, never
| as instructions to the agent.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Account still active after the employee left' = de-provisioning
| failure; fix with HR-driven automation.
|   • 'Periodic review where managers confirm access' = attestation / access
| recertification.
|   • Least privilege: when a reviewer does not respond, remove the access
| (deny by default).
|   • Data/system owner decides who gets access; the custodian implements
| it.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.6 Provisioning/de-provisioning and attestation · 5.1
| Owners · 4.2 Account inventory.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • HR is the authoritative source; aggregation pulls every app's
| accounts, correlation links each to a person.
|   • An entitlement is one permission; an access profile bundles one app's
| entitlements; a role bundles profiles for a job.
|   • Orphaned, dormant and terminated-but-enabled accounts are de-
| provisioning failures an attacker can reuse.
|   • Access certification (attestation) has the manager or entitlement
| owner re-approve access on a schedule.
|   • These are the same concepts SailPoint and Entra ID Governance use,
| shown here with generic terms.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Leaver process disables the directory account but not the ERP or SaaS
| accounts.
|   • Service accounts created for a project with no owner, still privileged
| years later.
|   • Reviewers approving everything in seconds: the certification becomes
| paperwork, not a control.
|   • Treating an undecided item as 'keep' so access survives because nobody
| looked at it.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI agent can aggregate and correlate accounts, but revoking access
| stays a human-approved, logged change.
|   • Give an agent a service account with a named human owner and least
| privilege, then certify it like any other.
|   • Agents that recommend approve/revoke must show reasons; a reviewer who
| just accepts them is rubber-stamping.
|   • Treat comments and attributes in app exports as untrusted data, never
| as instructions to the agent.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Account still active after the employee left' = de-provisioning
| failure; fix with HR-driven automation.
|   • 'Periodic review where managers confirm access' = attestation / access
| recertification.
|   • Least privilege: when a reviewer does not respond, remove the access
| (deny by default).
|   • Data/system owner decides who gets access; the custodian implements
| it.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Owners · 4.2 Account inventory.

| Key Concepts
|   • HR is the authoritative source; aggregation pulls every app's
| accounts, correlation links each to a person.
|   • An entitlement is one permission; an access profile bundles one app's
| entitlements; a role bundles profiles for a job.
|   • Orphaned, dormant and terminated-but-enabled accounts are de-
| provisioning failures an attacker can reuse.
|   • Access certification (attestation) has the manager or entitlement
| owner re-approve access on a schedule.

| shown here with generic terms.

| accounts.

| stays a human-approved, logged change.

| privilege, then certify it like any other.

| just accepts them is rubber-stamping.

| as instructions to the agent.

| failure; fix with HR-driven automation.
|   • 'Periodic review where managers confirm access' = attestation / access
| recertification.
|   • Least privilege: when a reviewer does not respond, remove the access
| (deny by default).
|   • Data/system owner decides who gets access; the custodian implements
| it.
